ox: Correct. The question asks only for the mean (average) reduction, so use only the two means from the Hypertrol row: 139.2 at baseline and 123.4 at 8 weeks. 139.2 − 123.4 = 15.8 mmHg.
Incorrect. 16.8 is one mmHg too large. It comes from a borrowing mistake when subtracting 123.4 from 139.2; the correct difference is 15.8.
Incorrect. 17.8 does not match 139.2 − 123.4. It is two mmHg too large and is not supported by any value in the table.
Incorrect. 18.8 does not match the table either. The standard deviations (11.9 and 10.5) are not part of the reduction and should not be added in.

concept.t: Reading and subtracting means from a results table
p: 'Mean reduction' means baseline mean minus follow-up mean for the treated group. Ignore SDs (spread) and the placebo row unless the question asks for a comparison.

bp968_0.trap: The standard deviations tempt you to use them in the calculation; the reduction uses only the means.
mem: Mean reduction = baseline mean − follow-up mean.
SD tells spread, not change.
Use the row for the group in the question (Hypertrol, not placebo).

fm.f: Mean reduction = baseline mean − 8-week mean, where baseline mean = Hypertrol group's average SBP at the start, 8-week mean = average SBP after 8 weeks
fm.why: The question asks how far the average fell, so we subtract the end average from the start average.

bp968_0.plain: Reduction is just 'how much lower did the average get': start number minus end number.

ox: Correct. High CO2, high H+ (lower pH) in active muscle lowers Hb's affinity for O2 (Bohr effect), so the curve shifts right and more O2 is released.
Wrong. Cooler temperature increases affinity and shifts the curve left. Trap: forgetting heat shifts right.
Wrong. Fetal Hb binds O2 more tightly than adult Hb, shifting the curve left so it can take O2 from mom. Trap: thinking fetal Hb unloads easily.
Wrong. CO binds Hb strongly and also makes remaining O2 bind more tightly, shifting left. Trap: assuming a poison lowers affinity.

p: The oxyhemoglobin curve shows how full Hb is with O2 at different O2 pressures. A right shift means Hb lets go of O2 more easily (lower affinity). A left shift means Hb holds O2 tighter.
Right shift: more CO2, more H+ (lower pH), higher temperature, more 2,3-BPG. These happen in working muscle, which needs more O2.

mem: Right shift: high CO2, H+, temperature, 2,3-BPG
Left shift: opposites, plus fetal Hb and CO
Right shift = lower affinity = more unloading
q34.mn: CADET face Right: CO2, Acid, 2,3-BPG (DPG), Exercise, Temperature all shift the curve right.
q34.trap: Mixing up which direction means higher affinity. Right = release.
q34.plain: Hot, busy muscles call out for oxygen, so the delivery truck drops off its cargo more easily.

ox: Correct. Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to keep Na+ and excrete K+. Water follows Na+, raising blood volume.
Wrong. Inserting aquaporins to reabsorb water is ADH. Trap: mixing up the two hormones.
Wrong. Decreasing Na+ reabsorption is ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide). Aldosterone does the opposite. Trap: reversing the direction.
Wrong. Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, mostly by transporters, not by aldosterone. Trap: picking the wrong segment.

p: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex. It acts in the distal tubule and collecting duct. It makes cells reabsorb sodium (Na+) and secrete potassium (K+).
Water follows sodium by osmosis, so blood volume and pressure rise. The renin-angiotensin system triggers aldosterone release when pressure is low.

mem: Aldosterone: Na+ in, K+ out, water follows
ADH: water only, via aquaporins
ANP: opposite of aldosterone
q35.plain: Aldosterone is a salt-saver. It tells the kidney to keep salt and water in the body.

ox: Wrong. Pepsin is the stomach protease, made from pepsinogen. It does not activate trypsinogen. Trap: choosing the most famous protease.
Correct. Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal lining cuts trypsinogen into active trypsin. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic zymogens.
Wrong. HCl activates pepsinogen to pepsin in the stomach, not trypsinogen. Trap: mixing up the two activations.
Wrong. Bile salts emulsify fats, breaking large drops into small ones. They do not cut proteins. Trap: confusing digestive helpers.

p: Pancreatic enzymes are made as inactive precursors called zymogens, so they do not digest the pancreas itself. Trypsinogen is one.
In the duodenum (first part of the small intestine), enteropeptidase cuts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and other zymogens (chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase).

mem: Enteropeptidase: trypsinogen to trypsin
Trypsin activates the other zymogens
HCl activates pepsinogen in the stomach
q36.trap: Choosing pepsin or HCl because they are the stomach's famous activators.
q36.plain: A safety cap keeps a tool locked. A key in the intestine unlocks the first tool, and that tool unlocks the rest.

ox: Wrong. Helper T cells release cytokines that direct B cells and others, but they do not make antibodies. Trap: confusing coordinating with producing.
Correct. Plasma cells are activated B cells that make and secrete large amounts of antibodies.
Wrong. Macrophages eat pathogens and show antigens to T cells. They do not secrete antibodies. Trap: assuming all immune cells do all jobs.
Wrong. NK cells kill infected or tumor cells directly, without antibodies. Trap: mixing innate and adaptive cells.

p: B cells are white blood cells of the adaptive immune system. When a B cell meets its antigen (a molecule it recognizes), often with help from helper T cells, it becomes a plasma cell.
Plasma cells are antibody factories. Antibodies are proteins that bind specific antigens. Some B cells become memory B cells for future infections.

mem: Plasma cell = secreting B cell
Helper T (CD4) = coordinate
Cytotoxic T (CD8) and NK = kill cells directly
q37.trap: Picking helper T cells because they are called the 'conductors' of the response.
q37.plain: A B cell is a recruit who learns the enemy's face. A plasma cell is the factory that mass-produces wanted posters for that face.

ox: Wrong. The stomach mostly churns and starts digesting protein. Only alcohol and a few drugs cross its wall well. Trap: thinking digestion and absorption happen in the same place.
Correct. The small intestine is lined with folds, villi and tiny microvilli, which create a huge surface area. Sugars, amino acids, fats, vitamins and minerals are absorbed here.
Wrong. The large intestine mainly takes back water and electrolytes and holds waste. Trap: picking the 'last stop' because it feels like the final step.
Wrong. The esophagus is only a tube that moves food by peristalsis (wave-like squeezing). Nothing is absorbed there.

p: Digestion means breaking food into small pieces. Absorption means moving those pieces into the blood or lymph. Most absorption happens in the small intestine.
Its wall has villi (finger-like folds) covered in microvilli (tiny hairs on each cell). These make a very large surface area, so nutrients pass into the body quickly.

mem: Small intestine = main site of nutrient absorption
Villi and microvilli = more surface area
Large intestine = water and electrolytes
Stomach absorbs almost nothing (alcohol, some drugs)
q38.trap: Do not confuse where digestion starts (mouth, stomach) with where absorption mostly happens (small intestine).
q38.plain: A paper towel with lots of folds soaks up more water than a flat sheet. The villi are the folds.

ox: Correct. Ca2+ binds troponin C. Troponin then shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads can attach and cross-bridge cycling starts.
Wrong. Ca2+ does not bind skeletal myosin heads. Myosin binds actin and ATP. Trap: assuming calcium acts on the 'motor' directly.
Wrong. Ca2+ does not bind actin itself. It acts through the troponin-tropomyosin complex that sits on actin. Trap: skipping the middle step.
Wrong. Calmodulin is the Ca2+ sensor in smooth muscle, where it activates myosin light-chain kinase. Skeletal muscle uses troponin. Trap: mixing up muscle types.

concept.t: Calcium and troponin in skeletal muscle
p: Actin is the thin filament. At rest, a rod called tropomyosin covers the spots where myosin (the motor protein) would grab actin. Troponin is a protein attached to tropomyosin.
When a nerve signal makes the sarcoplasmic reticulum release Ca2+, Ca2+ binds troponin. The rod moves aside, the spots open, and myosin can bind and pull.

mem: Skeletal: Ca2+ binds troponin, tropomyosin moves
Smooth: Ca2+ binds calmodulin
ATP binding releases myosin from actin; Pi release drives the power stroke
q39.trap: Skeletal muscle uses troponin; calmodulin belongs to smooth muscle. Also, calcium never binds myosin or actin directly.
q39.plain: Tropomyosin is a gate cover over the handholds on a climbing wall. Calcium is the key that moves the cover so climbers (myosin) can grab on.

ox: Correct. The passage says the trial was a double-blind, randomized controlled trial, and that participants were randomly assigned to Hypertrol or placebo. That is the definition of an RCT.
Wrong. A cohort study follows groups defined by exposure that already occurs naturally. Here the investigators assigned the drug at random, which makes it an experiment.

Wrong. A case-control study starts with people who have a disease (cases) and compares them to people who do not (controls). This study started with people with stage 1 hypertension and gave them treatment.
Wrong. A cross-sectional study measures everyone at one point in time. This study measured blood pressure at baseline and again at 8 weeks.

p: In a randomized controlled trial, researchers assign people to treatment or control by chance and then compare outcomes. Random assignment helps make the groups alike. Double-blind means neither the participants nor the researchers know who got which.
In observational studies, researchers do not assign anything; they just watch.

bp968_1.plain: Drawing names from a hat to decide who gets the real pill is randomization.
mem: Random assignment + control group = RCT.
Cohort: follow exposed and unexposed groups forward.
Case-control: start with disease, look backward.
Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time.
bp968_1.trap: Picking an observational design because blood pressure was measured; the key words are randomly assigned and double-blind.

ox: Correct. Percent reduction = (change / baseline) x 100. The change is 139.2 - 123.4 = 15.8 mmHg, and the baseline mean is 139.2. So 15.8 / 139.2 is about 0.114, or 11.4%.
Wrong. 12.2% is too high. It would require a change of about 17 mmHg on a baseline of 139.2, but the table shows 15.8.
Wrong. 13.0% is too high. 13% of 139.2 is about 18 mmHg, larger than the 15.8 mmHg drop.
Wrong. 13.8% is too high. 13.8% of 139.2 is about 19 mmHg, which does not match the 15.8 mmHg drop.

p: A percent change tells you how big the change is compared with where you started. Divide the change by the starting value, then multiply by 100.
Here the starting value is the baseline mean, 139.2 mmHg, not the 8-week value.

bp968_2.plain: Losing 15 dollars out of 140 is a small slice, about a tenth of what you had.
mem: Percent change = change / starting value x 100.
Divide by the baseline, not the follow-up.
Estimate: 10% of 139.2 is about 14.

fm.f: Percent reduction = (baseline mean - follow-up mean) / baseline mean x 100
fm.why: The question asks for the drop as a share of the starting blood pressure.
fm.nc: 10% of 139 is about 14; 15.8 is a bit more than 14, so slightly above 10%, about 11%.

bp968_2.sc: Check bounds: 12% of 139.2 is about 16.7, which is more than 15.8, so the answer must be under 12%.
bp968_2.trap: Dividing by the follow-up mean or picking a larger option without checking against 15.8.

ox: Wrong. This statement is supported. 139.2 - 123.4 = 15.8, which is about 16 mmHg. The question asks for the one NOT supported.
Wrong. This statement is supported. 138.5 - 136.7 = 1.8 mmHg for placebo, so the question's NOT-supported answer is elsewhere.
Wrong. This statement is supported. The Hypertrol drop (15.8) is larger than the placebo drop (1.8).
Correct. Table 1 shows only group means and SDs. A group mean fall does not show that every single person improved; some individuals may have had no change or an increase.

p: A mean describes a group as a whole. It does not tell you what happened to each person. The SD tells you values vary around the mean.
So a claim about 'every individual' cannot be backed by a table of means.

bp968_3.plain: If a class average improves, you cannot say every student improved.
mem: Means describe groups, not each person.
Read the question stem: NOT supported means find the false one.
Check each statement against the table with simple subtraction.

fm.f: Change = baseline mean - 8-week mean, where baseline mean = starting average SBP and 8-week mean = average SBP at the end
fm.why: These checks confirm statements A, B and C are supported.

bp968_3.trap: Over-generalizing from a group average to every individual; also missing the word NOT in the question.

ox: Wrong. 15.8 mmHg is the raw Hypertrol change (139.2 - 123.4) and ignores the placebo change of 1.8 mmHg. The question asks for the placebo-adjusted value.
Wrong. 1.8 mmHg is the placebo group's change (138.5 - 136.7) alone, not the difference between groups.
Correct. Hypertrol change = 139.2 - 123.4 = 15.8 mmHg; placebo change = 138.5 - 136.7 = 1.8 mmHg. Subtracting gives 15.8 - 1.8 = 14.0 mmHg.
Wrong. 17.6 mmHg comes from adding 15.8 and 1.8. The question says to subtract the placebo change.

p: Some of the change in a treatment group happens even without the drug (for example, relaxing, or the placebo effect). The placebo group shows how big that change is.
Subtracting the placebo change from the drug change leaves the part of the effect caused by the drug.

bp968_4.plain: If you and a friend both improved your jump after a warm-up, but you also used new shoes, the shoe effect is your gain minus your friend's gain.
mem: Adjusted effect = drug change - placebo change.
Subtract, do not add.
Find each group's change first, then compare.

fm.f: Adjusted reduction = (Hypertrol baseline - Hypertrol 8-week) - (placebo baseline - placebo 8-week)
fm.why: It removes the change that happened without the drug.

bp968_4.trap: Stopping at the raw Hypertrol change (15.8) or adding instead of subtracting.

ox: Correct. The table lists Delta CRP as 1.8 mg/L for Group A, 2.5 for Group B and 3.9 for Group C. Group A has the smallest rise.
Wrong. Group B's Delta CRP is 2.5 mg/L, which is higher than Group A's 1.8.
Wrong. Group C (placebo) has the largest rise, 3.9 mg/L, not the smallest.
Wrong. The values (1.8, 2.5 and 3.9) are different, so the groups did not have the same change.

p: Delta (the triangle symbol) means change. Delta CRP is how much C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation, rose after exercise.
A smaller rise means less inflammation. Compare the numbers across the three columns and pick the smallest.

bp970_0.plain: Like comparing three runners' times: smallest number wins when you want the quickest.
mem: Delta means change.
CRP is a marker of inflammation; CK is a marker of muscle damage.
For 'smallest', scan all columns before answering.
bp970_0.trap: Treating a larger Delta CRP as better. It means more inflammation.

ox: Correct. Random assignment gives each participant an equal chance of landing in any group, so differences such as baseline fitness tend to spread evenly across groups. The passage states that 30 participants were randomly assigned to each of three groups.
Wrong. A standardized treadmill protocol makes the exercise the same for all, but it does not balance out differences in how fit people already are.
Wrong. Measuring baseline CK and CRP lets researchers see changes, but it does not make the groups equal in fitness.
Wrong. Identical nutrition controls diet, a different variable. It does not balance baseline fitness.

p: People differ in many ways, such as fitness. If you let people pick their groups, the fittest might end up together and confuse your results. Randomization means chance decides.
With chance in charge, known and unknown differences tend to balance out between groups.

bp970_1.plain: Dealing cards to teams spreads the strong and weak players around without anyone choosing.
mem: Randomization controls confounders, including unknown ones.
Standardization controls the procedure, not the people.
Larger groups balance better by chance.
bp970_1.trap: Confusing keeping the procedure the same (standardization) with balancing the participants (randomization).

ox: Correct. Average = total / number of participants = 1,356 / 30. 30 x 45 = 1,350, and the leftover 6 / 30 = 0.2, so the average is 45.2 U/L. This matches the Group A Delta CK in the table.
Wrong. 45.6 x 30 would be 1,368, which is more than 1,356.
Wrong. 46.0 x 30 would be 1,380, which is more than 1,356.
Wrong. 47.2 x 30 would be 1,416, well above 1,356.

p: A mean is the total divided by how many people there are. Group A has 30 participants, according to the passage.
You can also work backward. Multiply an answer choice by 30 and see if you get the total.

bp970_2.plain: If 30 friends share a bill of 1,356 dollars, each pays 1,356 divided by 30.
mem: Mean = total / n.
Use n for that group only (30 here).
Check by multiplying back.

fm.f: Mean = total rise / n, where total rise = sum of all participants' rises and n = number in the group
fm.why: The question gives a total and asks for a per-person average.

bp970_2.sc: Multiply each option by 30: only 45.2 x 30 = 1,356.
bp970_2.trap: Dividing by 90 (all participants) instead of 30, or picking a value that does not multiply back to the total.

ox: Wrong. This is an accurate reading: Group A has the shortest mean recovery time, 12.4 min, versus 14.7 and 18.3.
Wrong. This is accurate: Group C, the placebo group, has the longest recovery time, 18.3 min.
Correct. The Delta CK values are 45.2, 58.9 and 72.4 U/L for Groups A, B and C. They are not equal, so the supplements did not affect CK equally. Saying they did is a misinterpretation.
Wrong. This is accurate: all Delta CRP values (1.8, 2.5, 3.9) are positive rises, so CRP increased in every group.

p: Questions like this ask which statement the data do NOT support. Check each choice against the numbers in the table.
Three of the four statements will match the table. The odd one out claims something the table contradicts.

bp970_3.plain: It is like checking a scoreboard: if someone says the teams tied but the board shows different scores, that claim is wrong.
mem: Test every option against the table.
Words like 'all' and 'equally' are suspicious.
Delta values are changes; positive means a rise.
bp970_3.trap: Choosing a true statement because the question is about misinterpretation; the false claim is 'equally'.

ox: Wrong. 5.0% is the false-positive chance for a single test. With three tests, the chance grows.
Wrong. 9.8% is for two tests: 1 - (0.95)^2 = 1 - 0.9025 = about 9.75%. There are three comparisons here.
Correct. Chance of no false positive across three independent tests is 0.95 x 0.95 x 0.95, about 0.857. So at least one false positive is 1 - 0.857 = 0.143, or 14.3%.
Wrong. 95.0% is the chance of no false positive on one test. It is not the chance of at least one.

p: Alpha = 0.05 means each test has a 5% chance of a false positive. When you run several tests, those chances stack up.
To find the chance of at least one false positive, find the chance of none (0.95 for each test, multiplied together) and subtract from 1.

bp970_4.plain: Each lottery ticket has a small chance, but buying three gives you more chances to win by luck.
mem: Familywise error = 1 - (1 - alpha)^k for k independent tests.
More tests means more false positives.
ANOVA with post hoc correction helps for 3+ groups.
3 groups give 3 pairwise comparisons.

fm.f: Familywise error = 1 - (1 - alpha)^k, where alpha = per-test false-positive rate and k = number of tests
fm.why: The question asks for the chance of at least one false positive across three tests.

bp970_4.sc: For small alpha, error is roughly k x alpha (3 x 5% = 15%), a bit lower: 14.3%.
bp970_4.trap: Picking 5% (one test) or 9.8% (two tests) instead of counting all three comparisons.

ox: Wrong. The table lists the HypoPress change as '-12.5', and the passage says 'mean change ... was –12.5 mmHg'. A negative change means the number went down, so this reads the minus sign backwards.

Correct. The table gives 'Mean SBP change (mmHg)' = -12.5 for HypoPress (SD 4.2). The minus sign means systolic pressure fell by 12.5 mmHg on average, which fits the passage's statement that HypoPress 'significantly lowers SBP'.
Wrong. A change of -12.5 is not zero. Only a value near 0 would mean no change, and even the placebo group moved by -2.3.
Wrong. +2.3 is not the HypoPress value. The -2.3 mmHg figure belongs to the placebo group, and it is also a decrease, not an increase.

p: A 'change' value is follow-up minus baseline. If the follow-up number is smaller than the starting number, the change is negative.
Systolic blood pressure (SBP) is the pressure in your arteries when the heart squeezes. For high blood pressure, a negative change is the goal, because the pressure went down.

bp980_0.plain: It is like a bank balance change: -12 means you lost 12 dollars. A negative sign tells you the direction, not that something is wrong.
mem: Negative change = decrease; positive change = increase.
Check which group a number belongs to before answering.
Placebo can also show small changes.
bp980_0.trap: Seeing a minus sign and thinking the value 'went up', or grabbing the placebo number (-2.3) instead of the HypoPress number.

ox: Wrong. Open-label means everyone knows who gets the drug, which allows expectations to change results. The passage says the trial was 'double-blind', the opposite of open-label.

Wrong. Randomization (passage: participants 'assigned' to HypoPress or placebo in a randomized trial) balances group differences such as age or diet, but it does not stop people from reacting to what they believe they are taking. That is blinding's job.
Wrong. A standard diet would be a way to keep one variable the same in both groups, but it does nothing about the belief that a pill works. The passage does not even mention diet.

Correct. The passage describes a 'double-blind' trial with a placebo. If neither participants nor investigators know who gets HypoPress, expectations cannot push the results either way, which controls the placebo effect.

p: The placebo effect is when people improve just because they expect to. A placebo is a fake treatment, such as a sugar pill, that looks like the real drug.
Blinding hides who gets what. Single-blind hides it from participants. Double-blind hides it from participants and investigators, so neither group's expectations can bias the results.

bp980_1.plain: It is like a taste test with unlabeled cups: if nobody knows which is the expensive brand, nobody's opinion can be swayed by the label.
mem: Blinding controls expectation bias (placebo effect and observer bias).
Randomization controls confounding (differences between groups).
Double-blind = participants and investigators both unaware.
bp980_1.trap: Picking randomization because it sounds like the strongest design feature. Randomization fixes group imbalance; blinding fixes expectation effects.

ox: Correct. Percent reduction = reduction / baseline x 100. The passage gives a mean change of -12.5 mmHg, and the stem gives baseline 140 mmHg. 12.5 / 140 is about 0.089, or 8.9%.
Wrong. 12.5% simply reuses the 12.5 mmHg change as if it were a percent. The change must be divided by the baseline of 140 first.
Wrong. 10.7% is too high. 10% of 140 is 14, and the reduction is only 12.5, which is below 14, so the answer must be under 10%.
Wrong. 9.5% is too high. 9% of 140 is 12.6, which is already slightly more than 12.5, so the answer must be a little under 9%.

p: Percent change tells how big a change is compared with where you started. You divide the change by the starting value (the baseline), then multiply by 100.
A change of 12.5 mmHg means something different if the baseline is 140 than if it is 400, which is why the division matters.

bp980_2.plain: Losing 10 dollars is a big deal if you had 20, and small if you had 1,000. Percent change shows that.

fm.f: Percent reduction = (baseline mean - follow-up mean) / baseline mean x 100, where baseline mean is the starting SBP and the numerator is the size of the drop
fm.v: drop = 12.5 mmHg (HypoPress mean SBP change -12.5), baseline = 140 mmHg (given in the question)
fm.why: The question asks for a reduction relative to the starting value, so the drop is divided by baseline.
fm.nc: 10% of 140 is 14 (too big); 9% of 140 is 12.6 (just over 12.5). So the answer is just under 9%, which is 8.9%.

bp980_2.sc: Test round benchmarks: 10% of 140 is 14 and 9% is about 12.6. The drop of 12.5 sits just under 9%.
bp980_2.trap: Reporting the raw mmHg change as a percent (12.5%) without dividing by the baseline.
mem: Percent reduction = drop / baseline x 100.
Never report the raw mmHg change as a percent.
Round benchmarks: 10% of 140 is 14, so 12.5 is a bit under 9%.

ox: Wrong. This statement is correct. A p-value below 0.05 is the usual cutoff for statistical significance.
Wrong. This statement is correct. A 95% confidence interval for a difference that excludes zero matches p < 0.05.
Correct. This statement is the incorrect one. A small sample gives low statistical power, meaning a real effect is harder to detect. It does not guarantee a significant result.
Wrong. This statement is correct. More participants reduce random noise (standard error), which raises power.

p: A p-value is the chance of seeing results at least this extreme if the drug truly did nothing. If p is below 0.05, researchers call the result statistically significant.
Power is the chance of detecting a real effect. Bigger samples give more power. Small samples give less power, so real effects can be missed.

bp980_3.plain: A tiny blurry photo makes it hard to spot a face. A larger, sharper photo (larger sample) makes the face easier to see.
mem: p < 0.05 = statistically significant (conventional cutoff).
95% CI for a difference that excludes 0 = significant at 0.05.
Larger n = more power; smaller n = less power.
The question asks for the INCORRECT statement.
bp980_3.trap: Missing the word 'incorrect' and choosing a true statement, or thinking small samples exaggerate or guarantee effects.

ox: Correct. The placebo group's mean SBP change was -2.3 mmHg (table), so blood pressure fell even without the drug. This is the placebo effect, and it is why HypoPress (-12.5) is judged against placebo. Net effect is 12.5 - 2.3 = 10.2 mmHg.
Wrong. A dose-response relationship needs several doses compared. The passage describes only one HypoPress group versus placebo, so it cannot show this.
Wrong. Randomization is how participants were assigned to groups. Comparing the two outcomes values does not illustrate how assignment was done.
Wrong. Adverse events (dizziness in 8% versus 3%) are reported separately. The SBP numbers measure blood pressure, not side effects.

p: A placebo group gets a fake treatment. Their results show how much change happens just from expectation, regular checks, and natural fluctuation.
To find the real drug effect, subtract the placebo change from the drug change.

bp980_4.plain: If everyone's grades go up a little just because a test is repeated, you need a comparison class to see what the new tutoring adds.
mem: Placebo group shows change without the active drug.
Drug effect = drug change - placebo change.
Dose-response needs multiple doses.

fm.f: Net drug effect = drug group mean change - placebo group mean change
fm.why: The placebo change is what happens without the drug, so subtracting isolates the drug's contribution.
fm.nc: 12.5 - 2.5 = 10, then add back 0.2 to get 10.2.

bp980_4.trap: Ignoring the placebo's own drop and giving the drug credit for the full 12.5 mmHg.

ox: Wrong. The table lists 132 mmHg for 5 mg, the highest of the four groups, so this is the least effective dose.
Wrong. The table lists 124 mmHg for 10 mg. That is lower than 5 mg but higher than 20 mg (117).
Correct. The table shows mean SBP of 117 mmHg at 20 mg, the smallest of 132, 124, 117 and 120. The passage also says 20 mg 'achieved the largest mean reduction of 18 mmHg'.
Wrong. The table lists 120 mmHg for 40 mg, which is 3 mmHg above the 20 mg group. The passage says 'no further benefit at the higher dose'.

p: A dose-response table shows how an outcome changes as the dose rises. Here, the lower the mean SBP, the better the drug worked.
More drug does not always give a bigger effect. Effects can level off or even reverse at a high dose.

bp983_0.plain: Like adding salt to soup: some helps, but past a point more doesn't improve it.
mem: Lowest SBP = best blood pressure lowering.
Scan every row; do not assume the biggest dose wins.
Plateau means extra dose gives no extra benefit.
bp983_0.trap: Choosing 40 mg because it is the highest dose.

ox: Correct. The passage says participants were 'randomized' to 5, 10, 20 or 40 mg and the study was double-blind. Random assignment balances other factors across groups, so differences in SBP can be attributed to the dose.
Wrong. A cohort study watches groups as they exist naturally and cannot assign doses randomly. Hidden differences (confounders) could explain the results.
Wrong. A case-control study starts with people who already have an outcome and looks back at exposures. It cannot show that a dose changed SBP.
Wrong. A cross-sectional study takes a single snapshot in time and cannot show that one thing came before the other.

p: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) assigns treatments by chance. Chance spreads age, diet and other factors evenly across groups, so the treatment is the main difference.
Observational designs (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) only watch what happens. They show association, but hidden confounders make causation hard to prove.

bp983_1.plain: Flipping a coin to decide who gets the treatment is like shuffling a deck so no group gets all the good cards.
mem: RCT = best design for causal inference.
Cohort follows groups forward; case-control looks back from outcome; cross-sectional is one snapshot.
Randomization controls confounding.
bp983_1.trap: Choosing cohort because the passage uses the word 'cohort' to describe the 200 adults. The design is what matters, and the passage says randomized.

Wrong. A cross-sectional study takes a single snapshot at one time. This study measured SBP after 12 weeks of therapy in groups assigned in advance, so it is not a one-time snapshot.

p: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is an experiment. Researchers use chance to place people into groups, give one group the real treatment and another a placebo (a look-alike with no active drug), and compare outcomes. Double-blind means neither participants nor staff know who got which.
Observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) only watch what happens. The researchers do not assign the exposure.

bp1074_1.plain: An RCT is a fair coin-flip contest between treatments. Observational studies are just watching a game someone else organized.
mem: Random assignment plus a control group means RCT.
Cohort: group by exposure, follow forward to outcome.
Case-control: start with outcome, look back at exposures.
Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time.
bp1074_1.trap: Choosing cohort because people were followed over time. Follow-up alone does not make a cohort study; the investigators assigned the treatment here.

ox: Wrong. 5% would be 7.5 mmHg out of 150. The actual difference is 10 mmHg, which is more than 5% of 150.
Correct. Percent lower = (control mean - high-dose mean) / control mean x 100. Table 1 gives Control 150 and High Dose 140, so (150 - 140) / 150 = 10/150 = 1/15, about 6.7%.
Wrong. 10% is the number you get by treating the 10 mmHg absolute difference as a percent. You must divide 10 by the control mean of 150 first.
Wrong. 20% would be a 30 mmHg drop from 150 (to 120). The table shows only a 10 mmHg drop.

p: A percent difference tells you how big a change is compared with a starting point (the reference). Subtract the two values, divide by the reference, then multiply by 100.
The question says lower than the control group, so the control mean is the reference.

bp1074_2.plain: Losing 10 dollars out of 150 is a small slice, not 10 percent of anything bigger.
mem: Percent change = difference / reference x 100.
The reference is the group named after 'than' or 'compared with'.
10 out of 150 is 1/15, about 6.7%.

fm.f: Percent lower = (control mean - high-dose mean) / control mean x 100, where control mean is the average SBP of the placebo group and high-dose mean is the average SBP of the 100 mg group
fm.why: The question asks how much lower one mean is relative to the control mean.
fm.nc: 10/150 = 1/15. Since 1/10 = 10% and 1/20 = 5%, 1/15 must sit between them, near 6.7%.

bp1074_2.sc: Test the options: 10% of 150 is 15 and 5% is 7.5. A 10 mmHg change lies between, so only 6.7% fits.
bp1074_2.trap: Reporting the absolute 10 mmHg difference as a 10% change. Always divide by the reference value.

ox: Wrong. This is supported: High Dose mean is 140 and Control mean is 150, so the high-dose group is lower. The question asks for the unsupported statement.
Wrong. This is supported: Low Dose mean is 140 and Control mean is 150, so low dose is lower than control.

Correct. This is NOT supported. Table 1 gives 140 mmHg for both Low Dose and High Dose, so the high-dose mean is equal to, not lower than, the low-dose mean.

p: In a NOT supported question, test each statement against the table one at a time. Three will match the numbers. One will not. That one is the answer.
The mean is the group average. The SD (standard deviation) measures how spread out individual values are; a smaller SD means values cluster closer to the mean.

bp1074_3.plain: It is like comparing four claims against a scoreboard and picking the one the scoreboard contradicts.
mem: Read the question stem for NOT or EXCEPT before you start.
Equal means are not 'lower' or 'higher'.
A hypothesis (dose-response) is not data.
bp1074_3.trap: Believing the stated hypothesis (high dose gives the greatest reduction). The table shows identical means of 140 for both treated groups.

ox: Correct. ACE converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Blocking ACE lowers angiotensin II, so less aldosterone is released. Wrong. ACE makes angiotensin II. Inhibiting ACE reduces angiotensin II production, it does not raise it.
Wrong. ACE also breaks down bradykinin. Inhibiting ACE means less breakdown, so bradykinin goes up (which explains the dry cough seen with these drugs). It does not go down.
Wrong. Aldosterone secretion falls with ACE inhibition, not rises. Less aldosterone means less sodium retention, so any sodium loss comes from lower aldosterone, not greater secretion.

p: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) raises blood pressure. Angiotensin I becomes angiotensin II through the enzyme ACE. Angiotensin II narrows blood vessels and triggers aldosterone, a hormone that makes the kidney keep sodium (and water) and dump potassium.
An ACE inhibitor blocks that step. Result: wider vessels, less aldosterone, lower blood pressure, and potassium that tends to rise.

bp1074_4.plain: ACE is a factory step; shutting it down means fewer of the pressure-raising products.
mem: ACE inhibitor: angiotensin II down, aldosterone down, bradykinin up.
Side effects: dry cough (bradykinin) and high potassium.
Aldosterone: keeps Na+, loses K+.
bp1074_4.mn: Drug names ending in -pril (such as lisinopril) are ACE inhibitors.
bp1074_4.trap: Thinking that a blood-pressure-lowering drug must lower bradykinin or raise aldosterone. ACE inhibition does the opposite for both.

ox: Wrong. The passage says the primary outcome was the change in systolic, not diastolic, pressure. Diastolic BP was only recorded among other measures.
Wrong. The proportion achieving SBP <140 mmHg is listed as a secondary outcome: "Secondary outcomes included the proportion of patients achieving target SBP <140 mmHg."
Correct. The passage states: "The primary outcome was the mean change in SBP from baseline to week 12."

p: The primary outcome is the main result a study was designed to test. Secondary outcomes are extra results examined alongside it.
Passages usually say outright which is which. Find the phrase 'primary outcome' and match it word for word.

bp1075_0.plain: The primary outcome is the headline of the story; secondary outcomes are the side notes.
mem: Search the passage for the words 'primary outcome'.
Everything measured is not primary.
Baseline means the starting measurement.
bp1075_0.trap: Picking a clinically important endpoint (reaching SBP <140) that sounds primary but is labeled secondary in the passage.

Wrong. Treatment length affects how large an effect may be, but any duration works if there is no fair comparison group. A 12-week course alone does not rule out confounders.

p: A confounder is a hidden factor, such as age or diet, that could change blood pressure and muddy the result. Random assignment spreads such factors evenly across groups.

bp1075_1.plain: Randomizing is like shuffling a deck before dealing, so no player gets a stacked hand.
mem: Randomization controls known and unknown confounders.
Placebo controls expectation effects; blinding controls bias.
More measurements do not fix an unfair comparison.
bp1075_1.trap: Choosing a design detail like duration that sounds important but does not make the groups comparable.

Correct. This is the trap. A 12-week trial can show short-term efficacy, but it cannot establish long-term safety or whether the effect lasts. Calling 12 weeks sufficient for long-term safety overreaches.

p: Short trials can show whether a drug works soon after starting, but rare or slow harms (such as kidney effects) may take months or years to show up.
Small samples also give less reliable results. Always separate the true strengths of a study, such as blinding and standard measurement, from claims that go further than the design can support.

bp1075_3.plain: A two-week test drive does not tell you how a car holds up after ten years.
mem: Short duration limits long-term safety conclusions.
Small n limits generalizability and power.
Standardized measurement and blinding are strengths.
bp1075_3.trap: Accepting that 12 weeks is enough to prove long-term safety. The statement claims more than the design can show.

Wrong. Chi-square tests compare counts or proportions in categories (for example, achieved target or not). The primary outcome here is a mean change, a continuous value.
Wrong. A paired t-test is for related measurements, such as the same people before and after. Drug and placebo groups are independent, so pairing is inappropriate.
Wrong. Correlation measures how two variables move together within one group. It does not compare the drug group with the placebo group.

p: Ask two questions. What type of data is the outcome: continuous (a number like mmHg) or categorical (yes/no)? And are the groups independent (different people) or paired (same people measured twice)?
Continuous plus two independent groups gives the independent two-sample t-test.

bp1075_4.plain: Comparing the average height of two different classes is a two-sample test. Comparing the same class before and after summer is paired.
mem: Continuous, 2 independent groups: two-sample t-test.
Same subjects measured twice: paired t-test.
Categorical counts: chi-square.
Relationship between two variables: correlation.
bp1075_4.trap: Seeing 'baseline and follow-up' and picking a paired test. The change score already removes baseline; the comparison is still between two independent groups.

A 95% confidence interval (CI) is a range likely to contain the true difference. If it does not include zero, the difference is statistically significant.

bp1076_0.plain: A CI is a net around the true value; if the net does not touch zero, there really is an effect.

95% CI excluding 0 for a difference means significant.
Placebo groups often show a small change.
bp1076_0.trap: Choosing the 20 mg dose as largest, or assuming placebo means no change. Read the exact numbers: 15.3 is the largest and placebo is 2.1.

Wrong. The 10 mg group's reduction was 8.4 mmHg versus 2.1 mmHg for placebo, with p <0.0001. Placebo was not as effective.

p: A placebo is a pill with no active drug. People given one may still see their blood pressure fall slightly, because they expect to feel better or because readings naturally vary.

bp1076_1.plain: A placebo group is like a speedometer calibration: it tells you what you would see anyway.
mem: Drug effect = drug change - placebo change.
Placebo change is not zero.
Blinding is judged by design, not by a small placebo response.
bp1076_1.trap: Reading any change in the placebo group as proof the drug does not work.

Wrong. 15.3 mmHg is the 40 mg group's mean reduction, which is a different row.

p: To find how much a drug adds beyond placebo, subtract the placebo group's mean reduction from the drug group's mean reduction.

bp1076_2.plain: If you grow 13 inches with fertilizer and 2 inches without, the fertilizer added 11.

Use the right row for each group.
The table's CI for 20 mg (8.6-12.6) contains 10.6.

Here the SD (standard deviation) is a measure of spread. Larger SD means the individual reductions varied more from the group mean.

List the means in order before judging claims.
Compare every number exactly.

Wrong. The 40 mg mean (15.3 mmHg) was larger than the 20 mg mean (12.7 mmHg).

So bigger doses give bigger effects, but with smaller and smaller added benefit.

bp1076_4.plain: Like adding sugar to coffee: the first spoonfuls change taste a lot, later ones barely do.
mem: Effect rises with dose but flattens (diminishing returns).
Compute step differences to see the pattern.
Doubling dose does not double effect.

fm.f: Step gain = mean reduction at higher dose - mean reduction at lower dose, in mmHg

Wrong. The placebo drop was 2 mmHg, smaller than the supplement drop of 14 mmHg.
Wrong. The passage says the researchers concluded the supplement significantly reduced SBP compared to placebo. No data say otherwise.

p: Systolic blood pressure (SBP) is the pressure in your arteries when the heart squeezes. Lower is better when it is high.
To compare groups, subtract the week 12 value from baseline in each group, then compare the two drops.

bp1080_0.plain: Like two students retaking a test: one gains 14 points, the other 2. The first improved much more.

Compare the treatment drop with the placebo drop.
A placebo group can change a little too.

fm.f: Reduction = baseline SBP - week 12 SBP, in mmHg
fm.why: The question compares the size of the change in each group.
fm.nc: Subtract in your head: 138 - 124 = 14, 136 - 134 = 2.

bp1080_0.trap: Thinking any change is a treatment effect. The placebo group dropped a little too, so compare the sizes.

Correct. Blinding means participants (and assessors) do not know who gets the supplement. The passage says the design included blinding, which limits expectation effects and biased measurement.
Wrong. Reporting percent reduction only describes the result afterward. It cannot control any bias.

p: The placebo effect is when people improve because they expect a treatment to work, even though they got an inactive pill.
Blinding hides group assignment from participants and assessors. Then expectations are the same in both groups and cannot tilt the results.

bp1080_1.plain: Like a taste test with the labels covered, so nobody's guess about the brand changes their score.
mem: Blinding controls placebo effect and observer bias.
Randomization controls confounders.
Placebo group plus blinding isolates the drug effect.
bp1080_1.trap: Crediting randomization for placebo control. Randomization balances groups; blinding handles expectations.

ox: Wrong. 1.5% is about the placebo group's reduction (2 out of 136). The question asks for the supplement group.

Correct. Percent reduction = (138 - 124) / 138 x 100 = 14 / 138 x 100. Since 10% of 138 is 13.8, the answer is about 10.1%.
Wrong. 14.0 is the drop in mmHg, not a percent. You must divide by the baseline 138.

p: A percent reduction shows the drop as a part of the starting value. Divide the drop in mmHg by the baseline, then multiply by 100.
The units cancel (mmHg divided by mmHg), so the answer is a pure percent, not mmHg.

bp1080_2.plain: If you lose 14 pounds from 138, you lost about one tenth of your weight.
mem: Percent change = change / baseline x 100.
Divide by the starting value.
10% of 138 is 13.8, a handy anchor.

fm.why: The question asks for the drop as a percent of the starting value.
fm.nc: 10% of 138 is 13.8, almost exactly 14, so the answer is just over 10%.

bp1080_2.sc: Find 10% of the baseline (13.8) and compare it with the drop (14).

Wrong. Ten participants per group is small, and the authors call for larger studies. No sample can rule out chance entirely.
Wrong. The supplement group fell 14 mmHg (about 10.1%) and the placebo group 2 mmHg (about 1.5%). The supplement group improved more.
Wrong. Baselines of 138 and 136 mmHg are nearly identical, and participants were randomly assigned. This points to similar groups, not different populations.

p: The placebo group shows what happens with no active treatment. Part of the supplement group's drop would likely have happened anyway.

bp1080_3.plain: If both teams improve, you look at how much more your team improved than the other, not just your own gain.
mem: Net effect = treatment change - placebo change.
Small sample means caution.
Randomization makes similar baselines expected.

fm.f: Net effect = supplement drop - placebo drop, in mmHg
fm.why: The placebo change is the background change that would occur without the supplement.

bp1080_3.trap: Reading the treatment group's change alone as the effect and ignoring the placebo response.

ox: Wrong. Clinical trials and observational studies answer different questions and complement each other. The study does not show one replaces the other.
Correct. The design used randomization, blinding and a placebo control to limit bias. Evidence-based medicine depends on such rigorous designs to give reliable evidence.
Wrong. One small study (n = 10 per group) cannot prove supplements are always effective, and the authors call for further research.
Wrong. The placebo group (SBP 136 to 134 mmHg) is what let the researchers see that the supplement fell much more. Placebo groups are essential.

p: Evidence-based medicine means making health decisions from well-designed research rather than guesses or tradition.
Randomization, blinding and a placebo group reduce bias. The stronger the design, the more we can trust the result.

bp1080_4.plain: Like picking a restaurant by many fair reviews instead of one friend's opinion.

One small study never proves something always works.
Avoid answers with always or never.
bp1080_4.trap: Overgeneralizing from one small trial or dismissing the placebo group.

concept.t: Reading a mean from a table
p: A mean is the average result of a group. Here it is the average drop in pain score, measured in millimeters (mm) on a pain scale. A bigger drop means more pain relief.
The standard deviation (SD) tells you how spread out people's results are. It does not tell you which group did best. To find the best group, compare the means only.

bp1081_0.plain: It is like comparing the average test scores of four classes: the class with the highest average did best, no matter how spread out the scores were.
mem: Mean = the average; the highest mean reduction means the greatest average relief.
SD measures spread, not size of effect.
Answer the exact column the question asks about.
bp1081_0.sc: Scan only the mean column and circle the biggest number: 18.7.
bp1081_0.trap: Getting distracted by the standard deviation column. A smaller SD does not mean a bigger mean.

ox: Correct. A placebo group gets an inert capsule that looks like the drug. Comparing the drug groups to it separates the drug's real effect from the placebo effect (feeling better because you expect to). The passage has only four drug formulations and no such comparison.
Wrong. A no-treatment group controls for natural change over time, but not for the placebo effect, because those people know they got nothing. It is a weaker control than a placebo.
Wrong. A high dose of a different known drug is an active comparator. It adds a different drug mechanism, so it does not isolate what the new drug itself does.
Wrong. A lower dose of Treatment C would test dose-response. It is still a drug group, so it gives no inactive baseline for comparison.

p: A control group is a group that is compared against the treated groups. A placebo is a fake treatment, such as a sugar pill, that looks real. Many people feel better just because they expect to. This is the placebo effect.
In this study, all four groups got a version of the drug. Without a placebo group, researchers cannot tell how much of the 10.9 to 18.7 mm pain reduction came from the drug itself.

bp1081_1.plain: To know if a new fertilizer works, you must also grow a plant with plain water that looks the same.
mem: Placebo = inert look-alike treatment that controls for expectation.
No-treatment controls do not control for the placebo effect.
Active comparators test which drug is better, not whether the drug works.
bp1081_1.trap: Choosing the no-treatment group or the known drug. Only the placebo matches the drug in everything except the active ingredient.

ox: Correct. Percent increase = (new - old) / old x 100. Going from B (15.2 mm) to C (18.7 mm) is an increase of 3.5 mm. 3.5 / 15.2 is about 0.23, which is 23.0%.
Wrong. 24.4% does not come from 3.5 / 15.2. It would need an increase of about 3.7 mm (0.244 x 15.2), which is not the table's difference.
Wrong. 27.6% would need an increase of about 4.2 mm on B's 15.2. The real difference is 3.5 mm.

The starting group goes in the denominator.

ox: Wrong. This is supported: C has the highest mean at 18.7 mm and the passage says C produced the greatest average pain relief.
Correct. This is the statement NOT supported. Table 1 gives B's SD as 4 mm and C's SD as 5.5 mm, so B had a lower SD, not a higher one.
Wrong. This is supported: D's mean of 10.9 mm is the smallest in the table.
Wrong. This is supported: every group has an SD above zero (3.1, 4, 5.5, 2.8 mm), and the passage says variability was substantial in all groups.

p: In a NOT question, three options are true according to the data and one is false. Your job is to find the false one.
Check each statement against the table one by one. Standard deviation (SD) measures how spread out the results are. A larger SD means more spread.

bp1081_3.plain: It is like spotting the one wrong fact in a list of four by checking each against the answer sheet.
mem: NOT questions: mark each option true or false, then pick the false one.
Larger SD means more variability.
Compare SD to SD and mean to mean; do not mix them.

ox: Wrong. The placebo effect needs a placebo group, and this study had none. All four groups received a formulation of the drug.
Wrong. Dose-response means changing the dose and watching the effect change. The passage says each person got a daily oral dose and the groups differ by formulation, not dose level.
