ox: Correct. The passage says "a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study", with participants "randomly assigned" to 10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg, or placebo.
Wrong. An observational cohort only watches people without assigning treatment. Here the researchers assigned doses.
Wrong. A cross-sectional study measures a population at a single moment. This study followed participants for 12 weeks.
Wrong. A case-control study starts from people with and without an outcome and looks back. Here participants were given treatments going forward.

p: In a randomized controlled trial, chance decides who gets which treatment. A placebo is an inactive look-alike. Double-blind means neither participants nor researchers know the assignments.
Mentioning that baseline traits were similar just shows randomization worked.

bp1101_1.plain: It is like drawing names from a hat to decide who gets the real pill, while nobody knows which is which.
mem: Assigned treatment plus random groups means an RCT.
Cross-sectional is one snapshot in time.
Case-control looks backward from the outcome.
bp1101_1.trap: Seeing 'baseline characteristics' and thinking observational. Comparing baselines is normal in trials.

ox: Wrong. 125% would come from mixing up the numbers, for example using 12.5 mmHg as if it were already a percent. The change is compared with placebo's 1.0.
Correct. Percent increase = (12.5 - 1.0) / 1.0 x 100. The difference is 11.5. Dividing by the placebo value 1.0 gives 11.5, so 1150%.
Wrong. 12.5% is just the 40 mg value (12.5 mmHg) relabeled as a percent. No comparison to placebo was done.
Wrong. 1% is just the placebo reduction (1 mmHg) relabeled. The question asks how much larger 12.5 is than 1.0.

p: A percent increase compares a new value with a reference value. Subtract the reference from the new value. Divide by the reference. Multiply by 100.
Here the reference is placebo, 1.0 mmHg. Because it is small, the percent is very large.

bp1101_2.plain: If you go from earning $1 to $12.50, that is 11.5 times more than you started with, an increase of 1150%.
mem: Percent increase = (new - reference) / reference x 100.
Divide by the reference, not the new value.
A tiny reference makes a huge percent.

fm.f: Percent increase = (40 mg reduction - placebo reduction) / placebo reduction x 100, where each reduction is the mean SBP reduction in mmHg
fm.why: The question compares the 40 mg group with the placebo group.
fm.nc: 12.5 - 1 = 11.5. Dividing by 1 changes nothing. Then times 100 gives 1150.

bp1101_2.trap: Skipping the comparison and reporting a raw table value as a percent.

ox: Wrong. The 10 mg group's SD is 3.1, which is larger than the placebo's 2.9.
Wrong. The 20 mg group's SD is 3.6, larger than 2.9.
Wrong. The 40 mg group has the largest SD, 4.3.
Correct. The SD column reads 3.1, 3.6, 4.3 and 2.9 (placebo). The smallest is 2.9, the placebo group.

p: Standard deviation tells you how spread out the individual results are around the group average. A small SD means people had similar results. A large SD means results varied a lot.
Find the smallest number in the SD column and read its row.

bp1101_3.plain: If every runner on a team finishes within seconds of each other, the spread is small. If they finish minutes apart, the spread is large.
mem: Small SD means tightly clustered data.
Compare the SD column, not the means.
In this table SD rises with dose: 3.1, 3.6, 4.3.
bp1101_3.trap: The 10 mg SD (3.1) is very close to the placebo SD (2.9), so a quick glance can lead to the wrong row.

ox: Correct. The means are 1.0 (placebo), 4.2 (10 mg), 8.1 (20 mg) and 12.5 (40 mg), so they rise at each step. This matches the passage: "a dose-dependent decrease in SBP".
Wrong. The placebo mean is 1.0 and the 10 mg mean is 4.2, so placebo was smaller, not larger.
Wrong. The 10 mg mean is 4.2 and the 20 mg mean is 8.1. They are not identical.
Wrong. The 40 mg SD is 4.3, the largest in the table. It is not the smallest.

p: A dose-dependent effect means that a bigger dose gives a bigger response. In the table, each higher dose has a larger mean SBP reduction.
Check each option by reading the numbers in the table, not by guessing.

bp1101_4.plain: Like turning up a volume knob: each notch makes it louder.
mem: Dose-dependent means the effect grows with dose.
Placebo means: 1.0 mmHg, small but not zero.
Check each option against exact table values.
bp1101_4.trap: Treating the 1.0 mmHg placebo response as almost equal to the 10 mg response of 4.2. They are clearly different.

ox: Wrong. The mean age is 45.3 years, much lower than 205.6.
Wrong. Mean systolic BP is 128.7 mmHg. It is a common focus in cardiovascular studies but is lower than 205.6.
Correct. Mean total cholesterol is 205.6 mg/dL, higher than 45.3 (age), 128.7 (systolic BP) and 128.4 (LDL).
Wrong. Mean LDL cholesterol is 128.4 mg/dL. That is lower than total cholesterol (205.6), which includes LDL.

p: The mean is the average. To find the highest mean, compare the numbers directly.
Units differ here (years, mmHg, mg/dL), but the question only asks which number is highest, so compare the numbers as given.

bp1106_0.plain: It is like asking which box has the biggest number written on it.
mem: Mean = average value.
Total cholesterol includes LDL, so it is always at least as large as LDL.
Scan all values before answering.
bp1106_0.trap: Choosing blood pressure because it is the topic of the study. The question asks which number is highest, not which variable matters most.

ox: Wrong. A cross-sectional study measures everyone at one time, so it shows association only. It cannot show that eating more caused higher pressure.
Correct. Randomly assigning people to different diets balances other factors (age, sex, smoking) across groups, so a difference in systolic BP can be attributed to caloric intake.
Wrong. A case-control study compares people who already have a condition with those who do not, looking back at exposures. It is prone to bias and cannot prove cause.
Wrong. An ecological study compares whole populations, such as countries. It is weak for cause because group averages hide individual differences and many other differences exist.

p: To show cause and effect, researchers must change one factor on purpose and see what happens. A randomized controlled trial does this: people are randomly put into groups and given different treatments.
Observational studies only watch what people already do, so hidden factors (confounders) can explain the link.

bp1106_1.plain: To find out if a new fertilizer works, you do not just look at gardens. You randomly assign it to some gardens and not others.
mem: RCT is the best design for causation.
Cross-sectional, case-control and ecological designs show association.
Randomization spreads confounders evenly.
bp1106_1.trap: Choosing the design the passage used. The passage reports associations, while the question asks about causation.

ox: Correct. CV = SD / mean = 12.4 / 128.7 = 0.096, which rounds to 0.10.
Wrong. 0.12 would need an SD of about 15.4 (0.12 × 128.7). The SD is 12.4.
Wrong. 0.15 would need an SD of about 19.3. The SD is 12.4.
Wrong. 0.20 would need an SD of about 25.7. The SD is 12.4, about half of that.

p: The coefficient of variation (CV) shows how spread out data are compared with their average. You get it by dividing the standard deviation (SD, a measure of spread) by the mean.
It has no units, so you can compare the spread of different measurements.

bp1106_2.plain: A 12 minute difference matters a lot on a 20 minute trip but little on a 2 hour trip. The CV captures that relative size.
mem: CV = SD / mean.
Put SD on top.
No units; multiply by 100 for a percent.

fm.f: CV = SD / mean, where SD = standard deviation of systolic BP and mean = average systolic BP
fm.why: The CV expresses spread relative to the average.

bp1106_2.trap: Flipping the fraction (mean / SD is about 10.4) or misplacing the decimal.

ox: Wrong. This is a valid interpretation. The passage reports that higher caloric intake was associated with elevated systolic blood pressure.
Wrong. This is valid. The passage states lower physical activity was associated with elevated systolic blood pressure.
Correct. This is NOT valid. The passage never says age is the sole predictor. It says diet and activity were associated with systolic BP independent of age and sex, which means other factors matter.
Wrong. This is valid. The passage concludes the associations were "independent of age and sex."

p: When researchers say a link is independent of age and sex, they adjusted for those factors. The link remains even after taking age and sex into account.
This does not mean age is the only predictor. It means age was not what explained the diet link.

bp1106_3.plain: Saying a runner is fast even when you account for height means height is not the whole story.
mem: Independent of X means adjusted for X.
Be careful with NOT questions: pick the false statement.
Words like sole or only are red flags.
bp1106_3.trap: Reading independent of age and sex as age is the only predictor. Also, it is a NOT question, so the false statement is the answer.

ox: Wrong. 116.3 to 141.1 is mean ± 1 SD (128.7 ± 12.4), which covers only about 68% of values.
Correct. About 95% of values in a normal distribution lie within 2 SD of the mean. 128.7 ± 2(12.4) = 128.7 ± 24.8 = 103.9 to 153.5 mmHg.
Wrong. 91.5 to 165.9 is mean ± 3 SD (128.7 ± 37.2), which covers about 99.7%.
Wrong. 126.5 to 130.9 is only about mean ± 2.2, roughly twice the standard error of the mean (12.4/√120 is about 1.13). That is a range for the mean, not individual values.

p: In a bell-shaped (normal) distribution, about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation (SD, a measure of spread) of the mean, about 95% within 2 SD, and about 99.7% within 3 SD.
This describes individual people. A confidence interval for the mean is much narrower because it describes the precision of the average.

bp1106_4.plain: If most people's commute is 30 minutes give or take 5, almost all fall within 20 to 40 minutes, which is two give-or-takes either side.
mem: Individuals use SD; the mean's precision uses SE.
95% range = mean ± 2 SD.

fm.f: 95% range = mean ± 2 × SD, where mean = average SBP and SD = standard deviation of SBP
fm.why: About 95% of a normal distribution lies within 2 SD of the mean.
fm.nc: Double 12.4 to get 24.8, about 25. Then 128.7 ± 25 is about 104 to 154.

bp1106_4.sc: Double the SD and add and subtract. Matching the endpoints to the options avoids long math.
bp1106_4.mn: 68, 95, 99.7 for 1, 2, 3 SD. Just memorize the three numbers in order.
bp1106_4.trap: Using the standard error (precision of the mean) when the question asks about spread of individual values.

ox: Wrong. The 10 mg group had a mean reduction of only 5 mmHg, the smallest of the three doses, so it cannot be the greatest.
Wrong. The 20 mg group had a 10 mmHg reduction. That is bigger than 5 mmHg but only half of the 20 mmHg seen at 40 mg.
Correct. The passage says the 40 mg group 'experienced the largest decrease of 20 mmHg', compared with 10 mmHg at 20 mg and 5 mmHg at 10 mg. The table row '40,20,5.6,25' agrees.
Wrong. Every dose lowered SBP (5, 10 and 20 mmHg), and each beat the placebo at 1 mmHg, so one dose clearly had the greatest reduction.

p: A dose-response table lists how big an effect is at each dose. Here the effect is the mean drop in systolic blood pressure (SBP, the top number in a blood pressure reading), measured in mmHg.
To find the greatest effect, scan the reduction column and pick the biggest number. Ignore the dose column, since a bigger dose does not by itself prove a bigger effect.

bp1107_0.plain: It is like comparing how many points three players scored: you look at the score column and pick the highest one.
mem: Mean reduction by dose: 10 mg = 5, 20 mg = 10, 40 mg = 20 mmHg; placebo = 1 mmHg.
Dose-dependent means a bigger dose gives a bigger effect.
Always read the exact column the question asks about.
bp1107_0.trap: Mixing up the dose column with the effect column, or picking the middle row by habit instead of comparing the numbers.

ox: Correct. The passage says participants were 'randomly assigned' in a 'randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design'. Random assignment spreads unknown differences (age, diet, genes) evenly across groups, which controls confounders best.

Wrong. An observational cohort study only watches people who chose or happened to get an exposure. The groups may differ in other ways, so confounders are not controlled. This study assigned doses by chance instead.
Wrong. A case-control study starts from people who already have an outcome and looks back at exposures. It is prone to bias and is not what was done here, since doses were assigned going forward.
Wrong. A cross-sectional study takes one snapshot in time. This study measured SBP at weeks 4, 8 and 12, so it followed people over time.

p: A confounding variable is an outside factor that is linked to both the treatment and the outcome, so it can fake or hide a real effect. For example, if healthier people picked the high dose, the drug might look better than it is.

Random assignment fixes this by letting chance decide who gets which dose. With enough people, groups end up similar. Blinding and a placebo group then guard against expectations and the placebo effect.

bp1107_1.plain: Dealing cards from a shuffled deck is fair; letting players pick their own cards is not.
mem: Randomized controlled trial = best control of confounders.
Double-blind means neither patient nor researcher knows who gets the drug.
Observational, case-control and cross-sectional designs cannot assign treatment, so confounding is a bigger risk.
bp1107_1.trap: Picking an observational design because it sounds more realistic. Realistic does not mean it controls confounders.

ox: Wrong. 5.5 mmHg is far below 35/3 (about 11.7). The means are 5, 10 and 20, and the 20 pulls the average well above 5.5.
Wrong. 8.0 is below the middle value of 10, yet the average of 5, 10 and 20 is pulled above 10 by the large 20 value.
Wrong. 10.5 is close to the middle value of 10, but the sum 35 divided by 3 is bigger than 10.5.
Correct. The three means are 5, 10 and 20 mmHg. Their sum is 35, and 35 / 3 is about 11.7 mmHg.

p: A mean (average) is the total of the values divided by how many values there are. 'Unweighted' means every group counts equally, no matter how many people were in it.
Here there are three dose groups, so you add the three group means and divide by 3. The placebo group is not included because the question asks only about 10, 20 and 40 mg.

bp1107_2.plain: Like averaging three test scores: add them up and divide by how many tests there are.
mem: Mean = sum of values / number of values.
Unweighted mean ignores group sizes; weighted mean uses them.
Check that the answer falls between the smallest and largest value.

fm.f: Unweighted mean = (m1 + m2 + m3) / 3, where m1, m2, m3 are the mean reductions of the 10, 20 and 40 mg groups.
fm.why: Each group counts equally, so we just average the three group means.
fm.nc: 35 / 3: 3 x 11 = 33, leaving 2 left over, so about 11 and two thirds, which is 11.7.

bp1107_2.sc: Estimate first: 35 / 3 is a bit more than 11 (since 33 / 3 = 11). Only 11.7 fits.
bp1107_2.trap: Averaging only two groups, dividing by the wrong count, or using the middle value 10 as the average.

ox: Wrong. This statement is true. The 40 mg group had SD = 5.6, higher than 4.1 (20 mg) and 3.2 (10 mg).
Correct. This statement is incorrect. The sample sizes are 35 (10 mg), 30 (20 mg) and 25 (40 mg), so the 10 mg group, not the 20 mg group, had the largest sample.
Wrong. This statement is true. The 10 mg group had the smallest mean reduction, 5 mmHg, compared with 10 and 20 mmHg.
Wrong. This statement is true. The 10 mg SD is 3.2, which is smaller than the 20 mg SD of 4.1.

p: Some questions ask which statement is incorrect. Check each option against the table and mark it true or false. Exactly one should be false.
Standard deviation (SD) tells you how spread out the individual results are. Sample size (n) is how many people were in a group.

bp1107_3.plain: It is like proofreading a list of facts: test each one and circle the one that does not match.
mem: Higher dose here meant larger SD (more variability).
bp1107_3.trap: Assuming the middle dose has the middle value for everything. Always read the actual n column.

ox: Correct. The reductions were 5, 10 and 20 mmHg at 10, 20 and 40 mg, so the effect rises with dose. The placebo group's reduction was only 1 mmHg, so each dose exceeded it.
Wrong. The 10 mg (5 mmHg) and 20 mg (10 mmHg) groups also beat the placebo's 1 mmHg, so the drug is not effective only at 40 mg.
Wrong. Every dose lowered SBP more than the placebo, so the drug was not ineffective.
Wrong. The 10 mg dose gave the smallest reduction (5 mmHg), so it cannot be the only effective dose.

concept.t: Using a placebo as the comparison
p: A placebo is an inactive treatment. Its group shows how much SBP changes even without the drug, because of expectation and natural variation.
A drug counts as effective if its group improves more than the placebo group. Here the placebo changed 1 mmHg, and every drug dose changed more.

bp1107_4.plain: If a plain-water group improves a little, a medicine only counts if its group improves clearly more.
mem: Compare each drug group with placebo, not with zero.
Placebo mean reduction = 1 mmHg.
Passage conclusion: dose-dependent lowering of SBP.
bp1107_4.trap: Looking only at the largest effect at 40 mg and ignoring that the lower doses also beat the placebo.

ox: Wrong. Placebo went from 140 to 138, a change of -2 mmHg, the smallest change in the table.
Correct. Drug A fell from a baseline of 140 to 120, a change of -20 mmHg. That is bigger than Drug B (-10) and placebo (-2).
Wrong. Drug B fell from 140 to 130, a change of -10 mmHg. That is only half of the Drug A change.
Wrong. The table shows -20 for Drug A and -10 for Drug B, so the reductions were not equal. The passage also says Drug A produced 'a greater average reduction'.

p: Baseline is the starting measurement before treatment. The change is the final value minus the baseline value. A negative change means the number went down.
To find the greatest reduction, compare the size of the drops: 20 is bigger than 10, which is bigger than 2. The more negative number is the bigger drop.

bp1108_0.plain: Like comparing weight loss: the person who lost 20 pounds lost more than the one who lost 10.
mem: Change = follow-up - baseline.
Drug A -20, Drug B -10, placebo -2 mmHg.
Bigger drop = more negative change.

fm.f: Change = week 4 SBP - baseline SBP, where baseline SBP is the starting value and week 4 SBP is the value at the end of treatment.
fm.v: Drug A: baseline = 140, week 4 = 120; Drug B: baseline = 140, week 4 = 130
fm.why: It measures how far each group's SBP moved.
fm.nc: All baselines are 140, so just compare the week 4 values: lowest is 120.

bp1108_0.trap: Picking Drug B because both drugs worked, without comparing the sizes of the changes.
bp1108_0.sc: All groups start at 140, so the lowest final SBP (120) wins.

ox: Wrong. A cross-sectional study is a single snapshot with no assigned treatment, so it cannot isolate the effect of a drug from placebo effects.

Correct. The passage describes a 'randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial'. Random assignment balances groups, and the placebo arm (change of -2 mmHg) shows the effect of just getting a pill, so the drug effect can be separated out.
Wrong. An observational cohort study only observes people and does not give a placebo. Differences between groups could come from other factors, not the drug.
Wrong. A case-control study compares people with and without an outcome by looking backward. It has no placebo group, so it cannot separate placebo effects.

p: The placebo effect is when people improve just because they believe they are being treated. To separate this from the drug's real effect, one group gets an inactive pill that looks identical.
Subtracting the placebo group's change from the drug group's change estimates the true drug effect. Randomization and blinding keep the comparison fair.

bp1108_1.plain: It is a taste test where no one knows which cup has the new recipe, so opinions are not swayed.
mem: Placebo arm = measures the placebo effect.
Blinding stops expectation bias.
Randomized controlled trial is the strongest design for cause and effect.
bp1108_1.trap: Choosing an observational design. Only a trial with a placebo group can separate drug effect from placebo effect.

ox: Wrong. -10 mmHg is the change for Drug B (140 to 130), not Drug A.
Wrong. -15 is not in the table. It is not the Drug A value or any group's change.
Correct. Table 1 shows Drug A with baseline 140 and week 4 SBP 120, a change of -20 mmHg.
Wrong. -25 is not in the table. Drug A dropped 20 points (140 to 120), not 25.

p: The mean change tells you how much the group average moved. It is the later value minus the starting value.
A negative sign means SBP went down, which is the desired result for a blood pressure drug.

bp1108_2.plain: If you start at 140 and end at 120, you moved down 20 steps.
mem: Change = final - baseline.
Drug A: 140 to 120 = -20 mmHg.
Negative = decrease.

fm.f: Change = week 4 SBP - baseline SBP, where week 4 SBP is the final reading and baseline SBP is the starting reading.
fm.why: It gives the size and direction of the movement.
fm.nc: 140 - 120 = 20, and the direction is down, so -20.

bp1108_2.trap: Dropping the negative sign or mixing up Drug A and Drug B rows.

ox: Wrong. this is a valid conclusion. The table shows Drug A at -20 and Drug B at -10, and the passage says Drug A produced 'a greater average reduction than Drug B'.
Wrong. this is a valid conclusion. The passage states the placebo decrease was 'likely reflecting regression to the mean'.

Correct. This is NOT valid. The study lasted only 4 weeks and measured only SBP, so it says nothing definitive about long-term safety. The passage itself says 'further studies are needed to confirm long-term safety'.
Wrong. this is a valid statement. The passage ends with 'further studies are needed to confirm long-term safety and efficacy'.

concept.t: What a study can and cannot conclude
p: A valid conclusion must be supported by what was actually measured. This trial measured SBP at baseline and after 4 weeks.
Safety over years was never measured, so claiming a drug is 'definitively safe' goes beyond the data. Watch for strong words like 'definitively' or 'always'.

bp1108_3.plain: A one-month test drive cannot prove a car will last ten years.
mem: Short-term efficacy does not prove long-term safety.
Absolute words (definitely, always, never) are often wrong.
Regression to the mean: extreme values tend to move toward average on retest.
bp1108_3.trap: Assuming safety from short-term efficacy data.
bp1108_3.sc: Look for the option with absolute wording that goes beyond the data.

ox: Correct. Systolic blood pressure is a well-established risk factor, and lowering it reduces the risk of stroke. This connects the trial's SBP drops (-20 and -10 mmHg) to broader cardiovascular benefit.
Wrong. The passage and Table 1 give no heart rate data, so a claim that Drug A raises heart rate is unsupported and does not link to risk reduction.
Wrong. Table 1 shows all groups had the same baseline SBP of 140, so this statement is false.
Wrong. This is true (only SBP was reported), but it describes a limit of the study rather than a link to cardiovascular risk reduction.

concept.t: Linking a measurement to disease risk
p: Systolic blood pressure is the pressure in your arteries when the heart contracts. Long-term high pressure damages blood vessels.
Because damaged or strained vessels can block or burst, high blood pressure raises the risk of stroke and heart disease. Lowering it lowers that risk.

bp1108_4.plain: Easing the pressure in a garden hose lowers the chance that it bursts.
mem: High BP is a major risk factor for stroke and heart disease.
Lowering SBP lowers stroke risk.
A surrogate marker (like SBP) is a measurement used to predict a disease outcome.
bp1108_4.trap: Choosing a true-sounding statement about the study that does not actually connect to cardiovascular risk.

ox: Wrong. The table shows ROS falling from 100 to 78, 55 and 32 as concentration rises, so it does not increase.
Wrong. ROS changed a lot, from 100 at 0 µM to 32 at 20 µM.
Correct. ROS drops steadily with each higher concentration: 100 (0 µM), 78 (5 µM), 55 (10 µM), 32 (20 µM). The passage also reports 'a dose-dependent reduction'.
Wrong. ROS at 10 µM is 55, lower than the 78 at 5 µM and 100 at 0 µM. There is no peak at 10 µM; the values only go down.

p: A dose-dependent effect means the response changes steadily as the dose rises. Here the dose is the concentration of Antiox-7 and the response is ROS, or reactive oxygen species, which are reactive molecules that can damage cells.
To spot a trend, read the numbers in order. If they keep going one direction, the effect is dose-dependent.

bp1109_0.plain: Turning a dimmer switch further and further makes the light steadily dimmer.
mem: Monotonic decline = dose-dependent reduction.
A peak means the values go up and then down.
bp1109_0.trap: Choosing a peak or no-change option without actually reading the numbers in order.

ox: Correct. In a cell-free assay there are no cells, so no enzymes can be switched on. If ROS still fall when Antiox-7 is mixed with a ROS-generating system, the compound itself is neutralizing ROS directly.
Wrong. Measuring SOD and catalase (cell enzymes that break down ROS) tests an indirect cellular mechanism. It cannot show direct scavenging.
Wrong. Plating more cells changes the amount of cell material but does not separate direct from cell-mediated effects.
Wrong. A higher dose of 40 µM in cells still has cells present, so any ROS drop could come from cell responses rather than direct scavenging.

p: A direct scavenger chemically reacts with ROS and removes them. An indirect effect works through the cell, for example by turning on protective enzymes.
To test a direct effect, take the cell out. If the compound still lowers ROS with only chemicals in a tube (a cell-free assay), the effect must be direct.

bp1109_1.plain: To test whether a sponge soaks up spills, try it on a spill on a bare table, not in a busy kitchen with helpers.
mem: Cell-free assay removes cell responses.
Direct scavenging = chemical reaction with ROS.
Good experiments change one thing to isolate a mechanism.
bp1109_1.trap: Choosing enzyme expression because it sounds relevant. It tests the alternative mechanism and cannot prove direct scavenging.

ox: Wrong. 18.4% is not (12.5 - 4.1) / 12.5. It is far too small, since MDA fell by more than half.
Wrong. 32.8% is the MDA that remains (4.1 / 12.5), not the amount lost.
Wrong. 48.8% would mean MDA fell to about 6.4, but the table shows 4.1 at 20 µM.
Correct. Control MDA = 12.5 and MDA at 20 µM = 4.1. Reduction = 12.5 - 4.1 = 8.4, and 8.4 / 12.5 = 0.672, which is 67.2%.

p: Percent reduction compares how much a value dropped to where it started. You find the drop (starting value minus new value), then divide by the starting value and multiply by 100.
The control group (0 µM) is the starting value here, because it shows MDA without the compound. MDA, or malondialdehyde, is a marker of damage to fats in cell membranes.

bp1109_2.plain: If a 12.50 dollar item goes on sale for 4.10 dollars, the percent off is the dollars saved divided by the original price.
mem: Percent reduction = (old - new) / old x 100.
Do not confuse the amount remaining with the amount lost.
Remaining % + reduction % = 100%.

fm.f: Percent reduction = (control MDA - treated MDA) / control MDA x 100, where control MDA is MDA at 0 µM and treated MDA is MDA at 20 µM.
fm.why: It expresses the drop relative to the starting level.
fm.nc: Dividing by 12.5 is the same as multiplying by 8 and dividing by 100: 8.4 x 8 = 67.2.

bp1109_2.sc: Quick estimate: 4.1 is about one third of 12.5, so the reduction is about two thirds, near 67%.
bp1109_2.trap: Giving the percent remaining (32.8%) instead of the percent reduction.

ox: Correct. If the fluorescent probe also responds to intracellular pH, then a lower fluorescence reading could reflect a pH change caused by Antiox-7 rather than a real drop in ROS. That would be a confounder of the measurement.
Wrong. TBARS specificity for MDA concerns the MDA measurement, not the ROS probe. Also, a specific assay is a strength, not a confounder.
Wrong. Using one cell line limits how far results can be generalized, but it does not create a false ROS result within this experiment.
Wrong. A 24 hour incubation is the same for every group, so it does not bias the comparison between concentrations.

p: A confounding factor is something other than the thing you are testing that can change your result. In an assay, a probe that reacts to more than one thing can give misleading signals.
A fluorescent probe gives off light when it meets ROS. If it also responds to pH, a pH change could alter the light and be mistaken for a ROS change.

bp1109_3.plain: If your bathroom scale also reacts to temperature, a cold floor could make it look like you lost weight.
mem: Confounder = a hidden factor that could explain the result.
Limited generalizability is not the same as invalidity.
Constant conditions across groups (like 24 hours) do not confound.
bp1109_3.trap: Choosing 'only one cell line'. That limits generalization but does not invalidate the ROS result.

ox: Wrong. This overstates the data. The experiment used cultured cells for 24 hours, so it cannot show that lower ROS 'directly prevent' atherosclerosis in humans.

Correct. MDA is a marker of lipid peroxidation (damage to fats by ROS). The table shows MDA falling from 12.5 to 4.1 nmol/mg protein, which suggests less lipid peroxidation, and lipid oxidation contributes to plaque formation in arteries.
Wrong. 'Always beneficial' is an absolute claim. These data come from one compound in cultured cells and do not show that all antioxidants always help.
Wrong. A single 24 hour cell culture treatment does not model chronic, years-long disease.

p: Oxidative stress is damage caused by too many reactive oxygen species (ROS). ROS can attack fats in cell membranes and in LDL particles, a process called lipid peroxidation. MDA is a leftover product that we measure to detect it.
Oxidized lipids help drive plaque buildup in artery walls (atherosclerosis). So lower MDA suggests less of this damage.

bp1109_4.plain: Rust on a pipe is damage from oxygen; measuring rust flakes tells you how much damage occurred.
mem: MDA = marker of lipid peroxidation.
Oxidized LDL contributes to plaque formation.
Cell-culture data cannot prove clinical outcomes.

Use the correct group and the correct two columns: Hypertensol baseline and Hypertensol 4-week.

bp1169_0.plain: If you averaged 138 points on a game and later averaged 120, you dropped 18 points.
mem: Reduction = baseline - follow-up.
Use the same group for both numbers.
Placebo's reduction here is 139 - 136 = 3.

fm.f: Reduction = baseline mean - follow-up mean, where baseline mean is average SBP at the start and follow-up mean is average SBP at 4 weeks.
fm.why: The question asks how far the Hypertensol group's SBP fell.

bp1169_0.sc: Check against the passage: it states 18 mmHg versus 3 mmHg.
bp1169_0.trap: Subtracting the wrong columns, such as placebo's values.

ox: Wrong. In an observational cohort study researchers only watch people and do not assign treatment. Here the investigators assigned participants to Hypertensol or placebo.

Wrong. A case-control study starts with people who already have an outcome (cases) and compares them to people without it, looking backward. Here the groups were assigned a treatment and followed forward.

Correct. The passage says participants were "randomly assigned to either Hypertensol (n = 100) or placebo (n = 100)" and followed for 4 weeks. Random assignment plus a control group defines a randomized controlled trial.
Wrong. A cross-sectional survey measures a group once at a single time. This study measured SBP at baseline and after 4 weeks of dosing.

p: In an experiment, researchers assign the treatment. In an observational study, they only watch what people already do.
A randomized controlled trial assigns treatment by chance and compares to a control group. It is the strongest design for showing cause and effect.

bp1169_1.plain: It is like a taste test where a coin flip decides which cup each person gets.
mem: RCT: random assignment + control group.
Cohort: follow groups forward, no assignment.
Case-control: start with outcome, look backward.
Cross-sectional: one snapshot.
bp1169_1.trap: Thinking a placebo group means case-control. 'Control' in an RCT is not the same as controls in a case-control study.

ox: Wrong. 11.0% would be about 15.2 mmHg of 138. The drop is 18 mmHg, so it is too small.
Correct. Percent reduction = (138 - 120) / 138 x 100 = 18 / 138 x 100, about 13.0%. By hand, 18 / 138 is close to 18 / 140, which is about 0.13.
Wrong. 14.0% would be about 19.3 mmHg of 138. The drop is only 18 mmHg.
Wrong. 15.0% comes from dividing 18 by the follow-up value 120. Percent reduction uses the baseline 138 as the denominator.

p: Percent reduction compares the size of the drop to the starting value. It tells what share of the original was lost.
Always divide by the baseline, because the starting value is the reference point.

bp1169_2.plain: If you owed $138 and paid $18, you paid about 13% of the debt, not 15%.
mem: Percent change = change / original x 100.
Denominator is the baseline.
Dividing by the smaller final number inflates the percent.

fm.f: Percent reduction = (baseline mean - follow-up mean) / baseline mean x 100.
fm.why: The question asks for the share of the starting SBP that was lost.

bp1169_2.sc: 10% of 138 is 13.8 and 13% is about 17.9, which is almost 18.
bp1169_2.trap: Dividing by the follow-up value (120), which gives 15.0%.

ox: Wrong. This is supported. Placebo baseline is 139 and Hypertensol baseline is 138, so placebo is 1 mmHg higher.
Correct. The passage says participants were randomly assigned to Hypertensol or placebo, but it never says who was blinded. Double-blind is not stated, so it is not supported.
Wrong. This is supported. The Hypertensol group fell 18 mmHg and the placebo group fell 3 mmHg.
Wrong. This is supported. The passage says n = 100 and n = 100, and the table lists 100 for both.

p: In a double-blind trial neither the participants nor the researchers who measure outcomes know who received the drug. This reduces bias.
A placebo does not by itself mean the trial is double-blind. The passage must say so.

bp1169_3.plain: It is like a taste test where nobody, including the server, knows which cup is which.
mem: Randomization is not blinding.
Placebo is not blinding.
Only accept design features the passage states.
bp1169_3.sc: For NOT questions, quote the text for each option. The one without a quote is the answer.
bp1169_3.trap: Assuming randomized and placebo-controlled means double-blind.

ox: Correct. Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors to narrow blood vessels (vasoconstriction) and to trigger aldosterone release, which makes the kidney keep sodium and water. Blocking AT1 widens vessels and reduces salt and water retention, so blood pressure falls.

Wrong. Blocking AT1 does tend to raise angiotensin II levels, because the loss of negative feedback increases renin release. But that extra angiotensin II cannot act at the blocked AT1 receptor, so it does not cause vasodilation. Angiotensin II normally causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation.
Wrong. Reduced bradykinin breakdown and cough are features of ACE inhibitors, which block the enzyme that makes angiotensin II. A receptor blocker does not act on that enzyme.
Wrong. The passage describes blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, not beta-1 receptors. Beta-1 blockers are a different drug class.

p: Angiotensin II is a hormone that raises blood pressure. It tightens blood vessels and causes the adrenal glands to release aldosterone, which makes the kidneys hold salt and water.
An AT1 receptor blocker stops the hormone from working. Vessels relax and less fluid is kept, so pressure falls.

bp1169_4.plain: It is like putting tape over a doorbell button: the signal can't be sent, so nothing happens.
mem: ARBs (names ending in -sartan) block AT1.
ACE inhibitors (-pril) cause cough through bradykinin.
Angiotensin II: vasoconstriction + aldosterone release.
bp1169_4.mn: ARB = Angiotensin Receptor Blocker. ACE = Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme.
bp1169_4.trap: Confusing ARBs with ACE inhibitors (bradykinin and cough) or with beta blockers.

ox: Wrong. The table shows HFD + Oxidex at 12.7 µmol/L, lower than HFD at 18.2 µmol/L. A lower number means a decrease, not an increase.
Wrong. The table lists p < 0.01 vs. HFD for the Oxidex group, which means the drop was statistically significant.
Correct. HFD = 18.2 and HFD + Oxidex = 12.7 µmol/L, a drop of 5.5. The passage states 'a 30 % reduction in MDA compared with the HFD group', and 5.5 out of 18.2 is about 30 %.
Wrong. Oxidex group = 12.7 µmol/L and control = 12.3 µmol/L. 12.7 is slightly above control, so MDA returned to near-control, not below it.

concept.t: Reading a treatment effect from a table
p: MDA (malondialdehyde) is a chemical made when fats are damaged by oxygen-related stress. More MDA means more damage. Mice were fed standard chow (control), a high-fat diet (HFD), or HFD plus the drug Oxidex.

To find a drug's effect, compare the drug group to the group that differs only by the drug. Here that is HFD vs. HFD + Oxidex. A p-value under 0.05 usually means the difference is unlikely to be due to chance.

bp1171_0.plain: If a spill makes a mess 18 units big and a cleaner shrinks it to 12.7, the cleaner helped a lot, but the room is still not cleaner than before the spill.
mem: Compare the treated group to the matching untreated group.
Lower MDA means less lipid damage.
Return to near-baseline is not the same as going below baseline.
p < 0.05 usually means significant.

fm.f: Percent reduction = (HFD mean - Oxidex mean) / HFD mean x 100, where HFD mean is the untreated high-fat group and Oxidex mean is the treated group.
fm.why: Percent change is always measured relative to the starting (comparison) value.
fm.nc: 18.2 x 0.3 is about 5.5, so 30 % fits.

bp1171_0.sc: When an answer choice matches a number the passage states outright, check it against the table quickly and move on.
bp1171_0.trap: Choosing D because 12.7 looks close to 12.3. It is actually slightly higher, so it is not below control.

ox: Correct. A dose-dependent effect needs several doses of the same drug compared against each other. The original study used 10 mg/kg/day, so adding 5 and 20 mg/kg with HFD alone as reference gives a low, medium and high dose. Randomizing mice keeps groups comparable.

Wrong. An observational cohort of patients does not control who takes the drug, and it uses people rather than the mouse model. It also has only one dose level versus none, so it cannot show dose dependence.
Wrong. A single dose cannot show how effect changes with dose. A cross-sectional study is also just a snapshot, with no comparison across dose levels.
Wrong. Comparing mice with and without atherosclerosis studies the disease, not the drug. Oxidex is not even varied in this design.

p: Dose-dependent means a bigger dose gives a bigger effect. To test it, you need at least three groups: no drug (or a reference), a lower dose and a higher dose. Everything else must stay the same.
A randomized controlled trial assigns subjects to groups by chance, which spreads unknown differences evenly. That makes it the strongest design for showing cause and effect.

bp1171_1.plain: To learn whether more sugar makes tea sweeter, you make several cups with different spoonfuls and taste them, not just one cup.
mem: Dose-response needs multiple dose levels.
Randomized controlled trials best support cause and effect.
Observational designs show association, not cause.
Cross-sectional means one snapshot in time.
bp1171_1.trap: Picking a design that sounds scientific but has only one dose or does not vary the drug at all.

ox: Wrong. 12 % does not match any comparison. The drop is 18.2 to 12.7, which is 5.5 out of 18.2, about 30 %.
Wrong. 20 % would mean a drop of about 3.6 (20 % of 18.2), giving about 14.6. The table shows 12.7, a larger drop.
Correct. Reduction = (18.2 - 12.7) / 18.2 = 5.5 / 18.2, about 30 %. This matches the passage statement of 'a 30 % reduction in MDA compared with the HFD group'.
Wrong. 48 % is the passage's increase of HFD over control (18.2 vs. 12.3), not the reduction caused by Oxidex.

p: Percent change tells you how big a change is compared with where you started. You divide the change by the starting value and multiply by 100.
The starting value here is the HFD group, because Oxidex is being compared with HFD alone.

bp1171_2.plain: If a $18 shirt goes on sale for $12.70, you save about $5.50, roughly one third off.
mem: Percent change = change / starting value x 100.
Use the comparison group as the starting value.
48 % in this passage is the HFD increase, not the Oxidex effect.

fm.f: Percent reduction = (HFD mean - Oxidex mean) / HFD mean x 100, where HFD mean is the high-fat group and Oxidex mean is the high-fat plus drug group.
fm.why: We want the drop relative to the untreated high-fat group.

bp1171_2.trap: Using the 48 % figure or dividing by the wrong group (12.7 or 12.3) as the starting value.

ox: Correct. The passage reports only plasma MDA (a marker of oxidative stress) and 'fewer lipid-laden macrophages'. Plaque itself was never measured, so 'may slow plaque formation' goes beyond the data.
Wrong. A larger sample usually makes results more reliable. Type I error (a false positive) is set by the significance level, not made worse by more subjects. If anything, n = 10 is small.
Wrong. The passage says the control group got standard chow. The HFD group is a separate group.
Wrong. Random assignment is a strength because it reduces bias. It is not a limitation.

p: A good limitation points out a gap between what was measured and what was claimed. A marker such as MDA is an indirect sign of damage, not the disease itself.
Randomization, blinding, controls and decent sample size are strengths. Do not pick strengths as limitations.

bp1171_3.plain: Measuring how many people carry umbrellas tells you about rain, but it does not directly measure how wet the streets are.
mem: Surrogate marker is not the same as the outcome.
Randomization is a strength.
Type I error is a false positive, tied to the p-value cutoff, not to a big sample.
bp1171_3.trap: Choosing an option that calls a strength (random assignment or a large sample) a flaw.

ox: Wrong. Control vs. HFD shows the effect of the high-fat diet (12.3 vs. 18.2), not of Oxidex.
Correct. These two groups both eat the high-fat diet and differ only in Oxidex. So the difference, 18.2 vs. 12.7 µmol/L, can be credited to Oxidex.
Wrong. Control (standard chow) vs. HFD + Oxidex differs in both diet and drug, so the effect cannot be pinned on Oxidex alone.
Wrong. Pooling HFD and HFD + Oxidex mixes treated and untreated mice. It differs from control by diet and drug together, and blurs the drug effect.

p: To test one factor, compare two groups that differ by only that factor. This is called controlling variables. Any difference is then attributed to that factor.
Here HFD vs. HFD + Oxidex differ only by the drug.

bp1171_4.plain: To test a new fertilizer, grow two identical plants in the same soil and light, and give fertilizer to only one.
mem: Change one variable at a time.
Pick the pair that differs by exactly one thing.
Control vs. HFD tests the diet, not the drug.
bp1171_4.trap: Choosing control vs. treated group because control sounds like the right baseline. It differs in diet too.

ox: Correct. Baseline SBP was 130 mm Hg and high-dose week-12 SBP is 117.3, a drop of 12.7, versus 2.5 for placebo. The authors report the high dose 'significantly lowered SBP' compared with placebo. Note that the table itself shows no p-value, so significance comes from the authors' conclusion.
Wrong. Low-dose reduction was 8.3 mm Hg (130 - 121.7), clearly larger than placebo's 2.5. The high dose was larger still (12.7). Nothing in the data says only the low dose was meaningful.
Wrong. Placebo SBP fell only 2.5 mm Hg (127.5 vs. baseline 130), the smallest drop. Low-dose fell 8.3 and high-dose 12.7.
Wrong. The SD for high-dose SBP is 3.7, which is small compared with a 12.7 drop and a 10.2 difference from placebo. It does not undermine significance.

p: Reduction = baseline minus week-12 value. A bigger reduction than the placebo group suggests the treatment works. Standard deviation (SD) measures how spread out individual values are.
If the difference between groups is much larger than the SD, the difference is unlikely to be random.

bp1172_0.plain: If one class improves by 13 points and a no-help class improves by 2, and scores only wobble by about 4, the help likely worked.
mem: Reduction = baseline - follow-up.
Compare treatment to placebo, not to baseline alone.
A difference much larger than the SD is likely real.

fm.f: Reduction = baseline SBP - week-12 mean SBP, where baseline is the starting average and week-12 mean is the average at the end.
fm.why: This turns the table's final values into reductions.
fm.nc: 130 - 117 = 13, then subtract the extra 0.3 to get 12.7.

bp1172_0.trap: Thinking a large SD automatically means no significance. Compare SD to the size of the effect.

ox: Wrong. The study was a parallel-group trial, not crossover. The passage says participants were assigned to one of three groups.
Correct. The passage says the trial was 'randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled'. Randomization balances groups, and blinding participants and investigators removes expectation bias.
Wrong. A wide range of baselines may help generalizability, but it does not reduce bias in measuring the supplement effect.
Wrong. Giving the supplement only to people who drop more than 5 mm Hg would select likely responders, adding bias.

p: Randomization means chance decides who gets which treatment, so groups are alike at the start. Blinding means people do not know who gets the real treatment. Double-blind means both participants and researchers are blinded.
Together they reduce selection bias and expectation bias.

bp1172_1.plain: It is like drawing names from a hat and hiding the labels on the bottles, so no one can tilt the results.
mem: Randomize to balance groups.
Double-blind hides assignment from participants and investigators.
Selecting responders adds bias.
bp1172_1.trap: Choosing generalizability, which is about external validity, not bias reduction.

ox: Wrong. 10.8 to 14.6 is 12.7 ± 1.9, a margin of about 1.9. With SE of about 0.6 (3.7 / 6.3), the 95% margin is only about 1.2, so this interval is too wide.
Wrong. 12.0 to 13.4 is plus or minus 0.7, which is too narrow. With SD 3.7 and n = 40 the margin is about 1.2.
Correct. 95% CI = mean ± 2 x SD/square root of n. Square root of 40 is about 6.3, so SE = 3.7 / 6.3, about 0.6, and the margin is about 1.2. 12.7 ± 1.2 gives 11.5 to 13.9.
Wrong. A zero-width interval would mean no uncertainty, which is impossible with SD 3.7.

p: A confidence interval is a range likely to contain the true average. Standard error (SE) = SD divided by the square root of the sample size. The 95% interval is about the mean plus or minus 2 SE.
More subjects make SE smaller and the interval tighter.

bp1172_2.plain: One sample average is a dart; the confidence interval is the circle around it that very likely contains the bullseye.
mem: SE = SD / square root of n.
95% CI is about mean ± 2 SE.
Bigger n gives a narrower CI.

fm.f: 95% CI = mean ± 2 x SE, where SE = SD / square root of n, SD is the standard deviation and n is the sample size.
fm.why: We need the uncertainty of an average, so we divide the SD by square root of n.
fm.nc: Square root of 40 is about 6; 3.7/6 is about 0.6; double it to get 1.2.

bp1172_2.sc: Margin is about 2 x SD / 6 for n near 40, so roughly SD / 3.
bp1172_2.trap: Using the SD directly as the margin and forgetting to divide by the square root of n.

ox: Wrong. This is supported. Reductions were 2.5 (placebo), 8.3 (low) and 12.7 (high), rising with dose.
Wrong. This is supported. DBP is 72.4 for the high dose and 75.6 for the low dose, so it is lower in the high-dose group.

Correct. The table has no adverse-event data. The passage only says adverse events were recorded and the authors saw a 'favorable safety profile', which is not the same as 'caused no adverse events'. So this is not supported.
Wrong. This is supported. Low-dose SBP is 121.7 and placebo is 127.5, so the low dose is lower.

p: For 'NOT supported' questions, check each option against the data. Three options will match numbers. One will claim something the data never show.
'Favorable safety' is a judgment. 'No adverse events' is an absolute claim that the table does not show.

bp1172_3.plain: A report card with only math grades cannot prove a student never misbehaved.
mem: Check each option against the table.
Absolute claims like 'no' or 'always' are often unsupported.
Absent data is not the same as no events.
bp1172_3.trap: Treating 'favorable safety profile' as proof of zero adverse events.

ox: Correct. Placebo week-12 SBP is 127.5 and high-dose is 117.3, so the difference is 127.5 - 117.3 = 10.2 mm Hg. Equivalently, reductions are 12.7 vs. 2.5, and 12.7 - 2.5 = 10.2.
Wrong. 12.7 is the high-dose reduction from baseline, which does not subtract the placebo response.
Wrong. 15.2 is 12.7 + 2.5. Adding the placebo response instead of subtracting it is the error.
Wrong. 2.5 is the placebo group's own reduction, not the difference between groups.

p: Even a fake pill can change blood pressure a bit. To find the effect due to the supplement alone, subtract the placebo response from the treatment response.
Both ways work: difference in final values or difference in reductions.

bp1172_4.plain: If everyone's grades rise 2 points just from retaking a test, only the extra rise counts as the tutoring effect.
mem: Placebo-adjusted = treatment effect - placebo effect.
Subtract, do not add.
Final-value difference equals reduction difference when baselines match.

fm.f: Placebo-adjusted difference = placebo mean SBP - high-dose mean SBP, where each is the week-12 mean.
fm.why: It removes the part of the change that a placebo also produces.

bp1172_4.trap: Adding 12.7 and 2.5 or reporting the raw reduction of 12.7.

ox: Wrong. Both doses show p < 0.01 versus control in the table, so Antiox-5 clearly has significant effects.
Wrong. The passage says 'both Antiox-5 doses were significantly different from the control (p < 0.01)', not only the low dose.
Correct. MFI falls from 1200 (control) to 860 (10 µM) and 660 (50 µM), both p < 0.01. The high dose gives a 45% decrease against NAC's 55%, and the passage says only the low dose differed from NAC.
Wrong. High-dose MFI is 660 versus control 1200, which is a decrease, so ROS goes down, not up.

p: ROS are reactive oxygen molecules that damage cells. MFI measures how much fluorescent signal there is, so a lower MFI means less ROS. An antioxidant should lower MFI.
A p-value below 0.01 means the difference from control is very unlikely to be chance.

bp1174_0.plain: Fewer glowing sparks on a screen means fewer harmful molecules around.
mem: Lower MFI means lower ROS.
p < 0.01 versus control means a significant effect.
NAC is a positive control, a known working antioxidant for comparison.
bp1174_0.trap: Missing that both doses are significant and misreading the NAC comparison.

ox: Wrong. The probe is how ROS is measured. It does not show that Antiox-5 caused the change.
Correct. The vehicle control gets everything except the drug (1200 ± 80 MFI). Without it you cannot tell whether the lower MFI in treated groups came from Antiox-5 or from the solvent or handling.
Wrong. MFI is the readout, not a way to prove cause.
Wrong. Triplicate replicates improve reliability, but they do not separate the drug effect from other factors.

concept.t: The role of a vehicle control
p: A vehicle is the liquid the drug is dissolved in. A vehicle control group gets only the vehicle. Any difference from treated groups is then due to the drug.
Replicates improve precision. Controls give causal attribution.

bp1174_1.plain: To test a medicine in juice, you also need a group that drinks plain juice.
mem: Vehicle control isolates the drug effect.
Replicates improve reliability, not causation.
Positive control proves the assay can detect an effect.
bp1174_1.trap: Choosing triplicate replicates because repeating sounds scientific. It does not isolate the cause.

ox: Correct. Reduction = (1200 - 660) / 1200 = 540 / 1200 = 0.45, which is 45%. This matches the passage statement of a '45% decrease'.
Wrong. 55% is the percent of control remaining (660 / 1200), and also the passage's NAC reduction. It is not the high-dose reduction.
Wrong. 30% would mean a drop of 360, giving 840. The actual drop is 540.
Wrong. 60% would mean 720 lost, leaving 480. The data show 660.

p: Percent reduction = drop divided by the control value, times 100. The drop is control minus treated. The control is the starting point for comparison.
Do not confuse percent remaining with percent reduced. They add up to 100%.

bp1174_2.plain: If a 1200-piece pile shrinks to 660, you removed 540 pieces, a bit under half.
mem: Reduction = (control - treated) / control x 100.
Percent remaining + percent reduced = 100%.
Divide by the control.

fm.f: Percent reduction = (control MFI - treated MFI) / control MFI x 100, where control MFI is the vehicle group and treated MFI is the high-dose group.
fm.why: It measures the drop relative to untreated cells.

bp1174_2.sc: Half of 1200 is 600. 660 is a bit above that, so the drop is a bit under 50%.

ox: Correct. This is the trap statement. A p-value below 0.01 only means the result is unlikely to be chance. It says nothing about whether the difference is large enough to matter clinically.
Wrong. This is a true statement about Tukey's test, not a trap in interpreting significance.
Wrong. This is also a true description of Tukey's test, so it is not a misleading statement.
Wrong. This statement is true and is the correct way to think, so it is not a trap.

p: Statistical significance means a result is unlikely to be due to chance. Clinical (practical) significance means the effect is big enough to matter in real life.
A tiny effect can still give a very small p-value if the study is large.

bp1174_3.plain: Proving a coin is slightly unfair does not mean the unfairness is big enough to change a game.
mem: Small p means probably not chance.
Small p does not mean a big or meaningful effect.
Tukey's test compares group pairs while controlling the error rate.
bp1174_3.trap: Equating a small p-value with importance.

ox: Correct. Mean MFI falls from 1200 (control) to 860 at 10 µM and to 660 at 50 µM, so a greater dose gives more ROS reduction. The passage notes 'a dose-dependent reduction in ROS levels'.
Wrong. The data show a clear relationship: 860 at the low dose and 660 at the high dose.
Wrong. Both doses are significant (p < 0.01), so there is no threshold with only the low dose working.
Wrong. The positive control is a single dose of a different drug, so it says nothing about whether dose matters.

p: A dose-response relationship means that as the dose goes up, the effect goes up, at least over a range. Pharmacologists use this as evidence that a drug causes the effect.
Here ROS fell more at 50 µM than at 10 µM.

bp1174_4.plain: A louder volume knob setting gives a louder sound, so you can trust the knob is doing the work.
mem: More dose with more effect is dose-dependent.
Need at least two doses plus a control to see it.
Positive control tests the assay, not the dose.
bp1174_4.trap: Using the positive control to argue about dose.

ox: Wrong. Placebo changed from 150 to 148, a drop of only 2 mmHg, the smallest change in the table.
Wrong. Low dose fell from 151 to 143, a change of -8, which is smaller than the -12 and -21 of the higher doses.
Wrong. Medium dose fell from 149 to 137, a change of -12. That beats placebo and low dose but not the high dose.
Correct. High dose went from 152 to 131, a change of -21 mmHg. The passage also says the high-dose group showed the largest mean reduction, and 21 is bigger than 2, 8 and 12.

p: Systolic blood pressure (SBP) is the top number in a blood pressure reading. It is the pressure in your arteries when the heart beats. Lower is better in hypertension, which means high blood pressure.
A reduction is how far the number fell. The table has a change column. A bigger negative number means a bigger drop.

bp1175_0.plain: It is like comparing four dieters by pounds lost, not by their final weights. The biggest drop wins.
mem: Reduction = baseline minus follow-up.
Compare the change column, not the baseline or week 4 values.
More negative change means a larger fall in blood pressure.

fm.f: Reduction = baseline SBP - week 4 SBP, where baseline SBP is the starting mean and week 4 SBP is the mean after 4 weeks of dosing
fm.why: The question asks for the size of the drop in each group.
fm.nc: Subtract 131 from 152: 152 - 130 = 22, minus 1 more gives 21.

bp1175_0.trap: Picking the group with the lowest final SBP or the highest baseline instead of the largest change. Here the high-dose group wins on change anyway, but check the change column.

ox: Wrong. Analysis of covariance adjusting for baseline SBP is a statistical step that corrects for different starting pressures. It does not stop people from expecting the drug to work.
Wrong. A 5-minute seated rest standardizes how SBP is measured and reduces random measurement variation. It does not hide who got the drug.

Correct. The trial is described as a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Neither participants nor investigators know who received drug or placebo, so expectations cannot shape reports or measurements.
Wrong. Reporting the proportion reaching SBP <140 mmHg is just a secondary outcome. Choosing what to measure does not hide group assignment.

p: Bias is a systematic push of results in one direction. Expectation bias happens when people believe a drug works and that belief changes what they report or how they measure.
In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who gets the real drug. A placebo is a look-alike with no active drug. Together they keep expectations equal across groups.

bp1175_1.plain: It is like a taste test where nobody knows which cup is the brand name. Nobody can be swayed by the label.
mem: Blinding limits expectation bias.
Randomization limits selection bias and balances groups.
Statistical adjustment fixes imbalance, not belief.
bp1175_1.trap: Choosing the statistical adjustment because it sounds rigorous. Statistics cannot undo expectation effects, only blinding can prevent them.

ox: Wrong. 9 mmHg does not come from averaging the four reductions (2, 8, 12, 21). Their sum is 43, and 43/4 is 10.75, not 9.
Correct. With equal group sizes the average is the plain mean of the table changes: (2 + 8 + 12 + 21)/4 = 43/4 = 10.75 mmHg. Placebo is included because the question says to include it.
Wrong. 13.7 is 41/3, the average of only the three drug groups (8 + 12 + 21 = 41). The question says to include placebo.
Wrong. 18 is close to the high-dose reduction of 21 alone. Averaging with 2, 8 and 12 pulls the result far below that.

p: A mean is the sum of values divided by how many values there are. When all groups are the same size, the overall average of the group means is just the simple mean of those numbers.
Here each group has one mean reduction: 2, 8, 12 and 21 mmHg. Use all four because the question includes placebo.

bp1175_2.plain: It is like averaging four test scores: add them and divide by four.
mem: Include every group the question names.
Equal group sizes means a simple average works.
Dividing by 3 instead of 4 is the usual slip.

fm.f: Average reduction = (sum of the four group reductions) / number of groups, where each reduction is the table change without the minus sign
fm.why: Equal group sizes let each group count equally.

bp1175_2.trap: Dropping placebo and getting 41/3, about 13.7, which is option C.

ox: Wrong. The table gives only baseline, after and change values. It has no p-value or confidence interval, so statistical significance cannot be read directly from it.
Wrong. Same problem: the table never states significance for the low dose. Not significant is also a claim the table cannot support.
Wrong. The medium-dose change of -12 is shown, but no test result is shown, so significance cannot be concluded.
Correct. The changes are -2 for placebo, -8 for low, -12 for medium and -21 for high. Each is a bigger reduction than the one before, which can be seen directly in the table.

concept.t: What a table can and cannot show

bp1196_1.plain: Shuffling a deck before dealing gives everyone a similar hand mix. Dealing hands by choice might not.

Wrong (this is supported). The passage lists n = 30 for placebo, low, medium and high dose groups.

bp1196_3.plain: A car that runs fine on a test drive of one week has not proven it will last ten years.
mem: Match each claim to the table or passage text.
Short trial = no long-term conclusions.
Absence of events seen is not proof of safety.
bp1196_3.trap: Reading "no serious adverse events" as "long-term safety established".

Wrong. Efficacy is the maximum possible effect (Emax). The question says both drugs have the "same maximal effect", so efficacy is equal.
Wrong. Half-life is how long the drug stays in the body. A dose-response curve does not measure it.

p: Potency is about how much drug you need. It is shown by where the curve sits left or right, and measured by EC50. A lower EC50 means more potent.

bp1196_4.plain: Two coffees give the same buzz at most, but one needs only a sip. That one is more potent.
mem: Potency = EC50 = left or right position.
Efficacy = Emax = height of plateau.
Lower EC50 = more potent.
LD50 and half-life are different ideas.
bp1196_4.mn: Potency = Position (left or right); Efficacy = Elevation (height).
bp1196_4.trap: Confusing potency with efficacy. Same maximum effect means equal efficacy, so only potency differs.

concept.t: Reading the main finding of a trial
p: The main finding compares the main outcome between the treatment group and the control (placebo) group. Here the outcome is the fall in systolic blood pressure (SBP), the top number in a blood pressure reading.

bp1197_0.plain: It is like two classes taking the same test: one got tutoring and gained 12 points, the other gained 3. The tutored class improved more, and the gap was too big to be luck.

p < 0.05 means statistically significant.
Only choose claims about outcomes the passage actually measured.
bp1197_0.trap: Option A names an outcome (diastolic pressure) the study never reported. Always check that the outcome in an answer was actually measured.

fm.nc: 12 - 3 = 9, so about 9 mmHg.

Wrong. The passage says the trial was double-blind, so more than participants were blinded. Blinding of participants alone also does not balance the groups. Randomization is the stronger answer.

p: A confounder is another factor that could explain the result, such as age or diet. Randomization means a chance process (like a coin flip) decides who gets the drug or placebo.

bp1197_1.plain: Picking teams by drawing names from a hat keeps the teams fair. Letting captains pick would let the best players clump together.
mem: Randomization balances known AND unknown confounders.
Blinding reduces bias in measuring or reporting; randomization reduces bias in who gets what.
Placebo control separates drug effect from expectation.
bp1197_1.trap: Blinding and a long follow-up sound impressive, but only randomization addresses confounding between groups.
bp1197_1.mn: Randomization is the key to cause: the draw from a hat makes groups equal.

mem: ARR = rate in one group - rate in the other group.

fm.f: ARR = P(drug) - P(placebo), where P(drug) = fraction of the Hypotensol group reaching a reduction of 10 mmHg or more, and P(placebo) = same fraction in the placebo group

bp1197_2.trap: Stopping at the placebo rate (0.15), or confusing ARR with relative risk reduction.

p: For a NOT-supported question, test each option against the passage. Three options will match a number or statement. One will go beyond it.
Words like comparable mean about equal. An answer that claims one group had more of something contradicts that.

Wrong. 0.94 comes from dividing 9.3 by the sum of the SDs (about 9.9). Cohen's d uses the pooled (average-type) SD, not the sum.

d = (mean 1 - mean 2) / pooled SD. A d near 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium, and 0.8 or more is large.

Use SD, not variance, and not the sum of the SDs.
d of 0.8 or more is large.

Reduction = baseline - follow-up.

bp1199_1.plain: If everyone gets a pill that looks the same, nobody can say "I feel better because I know I got the good one."

concept.t: Claims the data do not support

concept.t: Reading a change from a table
p: A mean change is the end value minus the starting value. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) is the pressure in your arteries when the heart beats. It is measured in mmHg (millimeters of mercury).
A negative change means the number went down. A positive change means it went up. Always check which group (row) you are reading.

bp1202_0.plain: It is like checking your bank balance: going from $150 to $140 means you lost $10.

A minus sign means a decrease.
Read the correct row (group) before picking the answer.

concept.t: Trend over time in two groups

mem: d = (mean1 - mean2) / pooled SD.
Equal n: pooled SD = sqrt((SD1^2 + SD2^2)/2).
Around 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large.

fm.f: d = (mean of placebo - mean of high-dose) / pooled SD, where pooled SD = sqrt((SD placebo^2 + SD high-dose^2)/2) because both groups have n = 30
fm.s: Pooled SD = sqrt((25 + 9)/2) = sqrt(17), about 4.12; d = (72 - 68)/4.12, about 0.97
fm.why: Cohen's d expresses the mean difference in units of spread.
fm.nc: sqrt(17) is just over 4, so d = 4/(just over 4), just under 1.

fm.f: Check: d must lie between 4/5 and 4/3 because pooled SD lies between 3 and 5
fm.why: The pooled SD is between the two SDs, so the answer is between these.
fm.nc: Only 0.97 is between 0.8 and 1.33 among the choices.

bp1220_2.sc: Pooled SD is between 3 and 5, so d is between 0.8 and 1.33. Only 0.97 fits.
bp1220_2.trap: Dividing by one group's SD or by the sum of the SDs.

ox: Wrong. This is supported. The high-dose mean is 68 bpm and the placebo mean is 72 bpm, so the high-dose mean is lower.
Wrong. This is supported. The passage states that all groups maintained similar baseline characteristics (age, sex distribution, BMI).
Correct. This is NOT supported. The trial enrolled healthy adults aged 20-45. The passage says nothing about adults over 65 or people with heart disease, so the result cannot be extended to them.
Wrong. This is supported. 72 - 68 = 4 bpm.

p: A study's results apply to the kind of people actually studied. Here that is healthy adults aged 20 to 45. Applying the result to a different group, such as older adults with heart disease, is an extrapolation.
On NOT-supported questions, find the option that goes beyond what the passage says about who was studied or what was measured.

bp1220_3.plain: If you test a shoe only on teenage runners, you cannot promise it works for elderly hikers.
mem: Results apply to the population studied.
NOT-supported answers usually extend to a new group or claim something not in the passage.
Check each option against the passage text and table.
bp1220_3.sc: Hunt for the option mentioning a group or condition the passage never mentions.
bp1220_3.trap: Assuming a good result in healthy young adults must hold for patients too.

ox: Correct. Between the low-dose (70 bpm at 5 mg/day) and high-dose (68 bpm at 15 mg/day) groups, RHR fell 2 bpm over an extra 10 mg/day. 2/10 = 0.2 bpm per mg/day.
Wrong. 0.4 is the slope from placebo to low-dose: 2 bpm over 5 mg/day. The question asks about low-dose to high-dose.
Wrong. 0.27 is about 4 bpm over 15 mg/day, the slope from placebo to high-dose. That uses the wrong endpoints.
Wrong. 2.0 is the drop in bpm, but it was not divided by the 10 mg/day increase in dose.

p: A slope tells you how much one thing changes for each one-unit change in another. Here it is the change in heart rate (bpm) for each extra mg/day of supplement.
Slope = change in y divided by change in x. Make sure you use the two groups the question names.

bp1220_4.plain: If a car drops 2 miles per hour of speed over 10 seconds, it slows 0.2 mph each second.
mem: Slope = change in outcome / change in dose.
Use the endpoints the question names.
The sign shows direction: a drop is negative.

fm.f: Slope = (RHR high-dose - RHR low-dose) / (dose high - dose low), where RHR is mean resting heart rate in bpm and dose is in mg/day
fm.v: RHR low = 70, RHR high = 68, dose low = 5, dose high = 15
fm.why: The question asks for the average drop per extra mg/day between two groups.
fm.nc: 2 divided by 10 is 0.2.

bp1220_4.trap: Using the wrong pair of groups or forgetting to divide by the dose difference.

ox: Correct. Table 1 lists the Hypertensol row as baseline 145, week 4 130, mean_change -15. That is 130 - 145 = -15 mmHg, a drop of 15.
Wrong. -10 mmHg does not appear anywhere in Table 1. The Hypertensol row gives a mean_change of -15, so -10 understates the drop.
Wrong. -5 mmHg is not in Table 1. The difference between 145 and 130 is 15, not 5.
Wrong. -3 mmHg is the Placebo row (146 to 143). The question asks about the Hypertensol group.

concept.t: Reading a change from a results table
p: A results table has one row per group. The mean change is the follow-up value minus the starting (baseline) value. A negative sign means the number went down.
Systolic blood pressure (SBP) is the pressure in the arteries when the heart beats, measured in mmHg (millimeters of mercury).

bp1222_0.plain: It is like checking your weight before and after a diet: you subtract the start from the end, and you read your own row, not your friend's.
mem: Mean change = follow-up mean minus baseline mean.
A negative change means a decrease.
Always match the row to the group named in the question.

fm.f: Mean change = week 4 SBP - baseline SBP, where week 4 SBP is the average after 4 weeks and baseline SBP is the average at the start
fm.why: The primary endpoint is the change from baseline to week 4.
fm.nc: 130 to 145 is 15 steps, and it went down.

bp1222_0.trap: Picking -3 mmHg, which is the placebo row, instead of the Hypertensol row.

ox: Correct. The passage states it was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: participants were randomly assigned to Hypertensol 10 mg or a matching placebo.
Wrong. In a cohort study, researchers only observe groups that differ in exposure. Here the investigators assigned the treatment (Hypertensol or placebo), so it is an experiment.
Wrong. A case-control study starts with people who already have an outcome and looks backward. This study assigned a drug and followed participants forward 4 weeks.
Wrong. A cross-sectional survey measures everyone once. Here SBP was measured at baseline and again at 4 weeks.

p: In an experiment, the researchers decide who gets the treatment. Random assignment makes the groups similar. A placebo is a fake pill that looks the same. Double-blind means neither the participants nor the staff know who got which.
In an observational study, researchers only watch what happens and do not assign anything.

bp1222_1.plain: It is like a fair coin flip deciding who gets the real medicine, with everyone kept in the dark about who got what.
mem: Randomization plus a control group = randomized controlled trial.
Double-blind: neither patient nor researcher knows the assignment.
Case-control looks backward; cohort follows forward without assigning treatment; cross-sectional is one snapshot.
bp1222_1.trap: Choosing cohort because people were followed over time. Following over time is not enough. Random assignment by the researchers makes it a trial.

ox: Correct. Percent reduction = drop / baseline x 100. The drop is 15 (145 to 130, from Table 1) and the baseline is 145. 15/145 is a little over 10%, so 10%.
